studyMetadata.title: 1 John for Today
studyMetadata.subtitle: Bible Study
studyMetadata.description:
Many people long for certainty in their faith. Can I really know God? Can I be sure I belong to Him? What does genuine faith actually look like? 1 John is written to answer those questions plainly and pastorally.
‘What we have seen and heard we announce to you too, so that you may have fellowship with us (and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ).’ (1 John 1:3, NET)
John writes as a witness, not a philosopher. He speaks of what he has seen, heard, and experienced. His message is simple but profound: real faith is not vague or uncertain. It is rooted in truth, expressed in love, and lived out in the light.

elements.text: The letter we call 1 John was written into a crisis. A group of people had left the community of believers — people who had seemed, perhaps, to be impressive and mature Christians. Their departure had left John’s readers shaken and confused. Could they trust what they had been taught? Were they really God’s children? Did they really have eternal life?

elements.question: 1 John is only five short chapters in length. Try, if you can to read (or listen to) the whole thing in one go…
elements.answer:
1:1This is what we proclaim to you: what was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and our hands have touched (concerning the word of life— 2and the life was revealed, and we have seen and testify and announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us). 3What we have seen and heard we announce to you too, so that you may have fellowship with us (and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ). 4Thus we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.

5Now this is the gospel message we have heard from him and announce to you: God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. 6If we say we have fellowship with him and yet keep on walking in the darkness, we are lying and not practicing the truth. 7But if we walk in the light as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin. 8If we say we do not bear the guilt of sin, we are deceiving ourselves and the truth is not in us. 9But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous, forgiving us our sins and cleansing us from all unrighteousness. 10If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar and his word is not in us. 2:1(My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin.) But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the Righteous One, 2and he himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for our sins but also for the whole world.

3Now by this we know that we have come to know God: if we keep his commandments. 4The one who says “I have come to know God” and yet does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in such a person. 5But whoever obeys his word, truly in this person the love of God has been perfected. By this we know that we are in him. 6The one who says he resides in God ought himself to walk just as Jesus walked.

7Dear friends, I am not writing a new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you have had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have already heard. 8On the other hand, I am writing a new commandment to you which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining. 9The one who says he is in the light but still hates his fellow Christian is still in the darkness. 10The one who loves his fellow Christian resides in the light, and there is no cause for stumbling in him. 11But the one who hates his fellow Christian is in the darkness, walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.

12I am writing to you, little children, that your sins have been forgiven because of his name. 13I am writing to you, fathers, that you have known him who has been from the beginning. I am writing to you, young people, that you have conquered the evil one. 14I have written to you, children, that you have known the Father. I have written to you, fathers, that you have known him who has been from the beginning. I have written to you, young people, that you are strong, and the word of God resides in you, and you have conquered the evil one.

15Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, 16because all that is in the world (the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and the arrogance produced by material possessions) is not from the Father, but is from the world. 17And the world is passing away with all its desires, but the person who does the will of God remains forever.

18Children, it is the last hour, and just as you heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. We know from this that it is the last hour. 19They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us, because if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us. But they went out from us to demonstrate that all of them do not belong to us.

20Nevertheless you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you all know. 21I have not written to you that you do not know the truth, but that you do know it, and that no lie is of the truth. 22Who is the liar but the person who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This one is the antichrist: the person who denies the Father and the Son. 23Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either. The person who confesses the Son has the Father also.

24As for you, what you have heard from the beginning must remain in you. If what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father. 25Now this is the promise that he himself made to us: eternal life. 26These things I have written to you about those who are trying to deceive you.

27Now as for you, the anointing that you received from him resides in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about all things, it is true and is not a lie. Just as it has taught you, you reside in him.

28And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink away from him in shame when he comes back. 29If you know that he is righteous, you also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been fathered by him.

3:1(See what sort of love the Father has given to us: that we should be called God’s children—and indeed we are! For this reason the world does not know us: because it did not know him. 2Dear friends, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that whenever it is revealed we will be like him, because we will see him just as he is. 3And everyone who has this hope focused on him purifies himself, just as Jesus is pure).

4Everyone who practices sin also practices lawlessness; indeed, sin is lawlessness. 5And you know that Jesus was revealed to take away sins, and in him there is no sin. 6Everyone who resides in him does not sin; everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him. 7Little children, let no one deceive you: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Jesus is righteous. 8The one who practices sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God was revealed: to destroy the works of the devil. 9Everyone who has been fathered by God does not practice sin, because God’s seed resides in him, and thus he is not able to sin, because he has been fathered by God. 10By this the children of God and the children of the devil are revealed: Everyone who does not practice righteousness—the one who does not love his fellow Christian —is not of God.

11For this is the gospel message that you have heard from the beginning: that we should love one another, 12not like Cain who was of the evil one and brutally murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his deeds were evil, but his brother’s were righteous.

13Therefore do not be surprised, brothers and sisters, if the world hates you. 14We know that we have crossed over from death to life because we love our fellow Christians. The one who does not love remains in death. 15Everyone who hates his fellow Christian is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life residing in him. 16We have come to know love by this: that Jesus laid down his life for us; thus we ought to lay down our lives for our fellow Christians. 17But whoever has the world’s possessions and sees his fellow Christian in need and shuts off his compassion against him, how can the love of God reside in such a person?

18Little children, let us not love with word or with tongue but in deed and truth. 19And by this we will know that we are of the truth and will convince our conscience in his presence, 20that if our conscience condemns us, that God is greater than our conscience and knows all things. 21Dear friends, if our conscience does not condemn us, we have confidence in the presence of God, 22and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do the things that are pleasing to him. 23Now this is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he gave us the commandment. 24And the person who keeps his commandments resides in God, and God in him. Now by this we know that God resides in us: by the Spirit he has given us.

4:1Dear friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to determine if they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. 2By this you know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses Jesus as the Christ who has come in the flesh is from God, 3but every spirit that refuses to confess Jesus, that spirit is not from God, and this is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming, and now is already in the world.

4You are from God, little children, and have conquered them, because the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world. 5They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world’s perspective and the world listens to them. 6We are from God; the person who knows God listens to us, but whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deceit.

7Dear friends, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves has been fathered by God and knows God. 8The person who does not love does not know God, because God is love. 9By this the love of God is revealed in us: that God has sent his one and only Son into the world so that we may live through him. 10In this is love: not that we have loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins.

11Dear friends, if God so loved us, then we also ought to love one another. 12No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God resides in us, and his love is perfected in us. 13By this we know that we reside in God and he in us: in that he has given us of his Spirit. 14And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent the Son to be the Savior of the world.

15If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God resides in him and he in God. 16And we have come to know and to believe the love that God has in us. God is love, and the one who resides in love resides in God, and God resides in him. 17By this love is perfected with us, so that we may have confidence in the day of judgment, because just as Jesus is, so also are we in this world. 18There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear has to do with punishment. The one who fears punishment has not been perfected in love. 19We love because he loved us first.

20If anyone says “I love God” and yet hates his fellow Christian, he is a liar, because the one who does not love his fellow Christian whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen. 21And the commandment we have from him is this: that the one who loves God should love his fellow Christian too. 5:1Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been fathered by God, and everyone who loves the father loves the child fathered by him. 2By this we know that we love the children of God: whenever we love God and obey his commandments. 3For this is the love of God: that we keep his commandments. And his commandments do not weigh us down, 4because everyone who has been fathered by God conquers the world. This is the conquering power that has conquered the world: our faith.

5Now who is the person who has conquered the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? 6Jesus Christ is the one who came by water and blood—not by the water only, but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth. 7For there are three that testify, 8the Spirit and the water and the blood, and these three are in agreement.

9If we accept the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, because this is the testimony of God that he has testified concerning his Son. 10(The one who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself; the one who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has testified concerning his Son.) 11And this is the testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. 12The one who has the Son has this eternal life; the one who does not have the Son of God does not have this eternal life.

13I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life.

14And this is the confidence that we have before him: that whenever we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. 15And if we know that he hears us in regard to whatever we ask, then we know that we have the requests that we have asked from him. 16If anyone sees his fellow Christian committing a sin not resulting in death, he should ask, and God will grant life to the person who commits a sin not resulting in death. There is a sin resulting in death. I do not say that he should ask about that. 17All unrighteousness is sin, but there is sin not resulting in death.

18We know that everyone fathered by God does not sin, but God protects the one he has fathered, and the evil one cannot touch him. 19We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one. 20And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us insight to know him who is true, and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This one is the true God and eternal life. 21Little children, guard yourselves from idols.

elements.text: 1:1–4: The testimony of the apostles proclaims the way to fellowship with God

elements.passageText: 1This is what we proclaim to you: what was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and our hands have touched (concerning the word of life— 2and the life was revealed, and we have seen and testify and announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us). 3What we have seen and heard we announce to you too, so that you may have fellowship with us (and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ). 4Thus we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.

elements.question: Why does John start his letter as he does? What is striking about these opening verses? Does it remind you of anywhere else in the Bible?
elements.questionHintFirst: Count the different senses and verbs John piles up before he reaches his main point.
elements.questionHint:
Notice how many different senses John mentions in just the first two verses.
What impression does that repetition create about the kind of claim he is making?
elements.sampleAnswer: John opens with an almost overwhelming accumulation of sensory language — “heard,” “seen with our eyes,” “looked at,” “hands have touched.” This is striking because it is so insistently physical and eyewitness-based. John isn’t passing on a tradition or a philosophy; he is announcing something he and others personally encountered. The opening almost certainly echoes the prologue of John’s Gospel (“In the beginning was the Word…”) and perhaps also Genesis 1:1 (“In the beginning…”). By starting this way, John is deliberately grounding everything that follows in the reliability of firsthand testimony about a real, historical, touchable person.
elements.mainPoint: John grounds the gospel in **firsthand, physical eyewitness testimony** to the eternal Son, echoing the opening of his Gospel.

elements.question: Notice how many times we/us/our appear in v1–4. Who is this referring to?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask who could say “we” about having heard, seen and touched Jesus.
elements.questionHint:
Look at how John switches between “we” and “you” in these verses.
What is the difference between those two groups?
Why does that difference matter?
elements.sampleAnswer: The “we/us/our” throughout v1–4 refers to the apostles — those who were eyewitnesses of Jesus’s earthly ministry and who personally heard, saw, and touched him. John is writing as part of this group, distinguishing himself and his fellow apostles from “you,” his readers, who did not have this direct encounter. The force of this is significant: when John writes, he is not simply sharing his personal opinion but speaking as one with firsthand authority. The apostolic “we” is the source of reliable testimony on which the readers’ faith can rest.
elements.mainPoint: The “we” is the **apostles**, whose eyewitness testimony gives their readers a secure foundation.

elements.passageText: 1This is what we proclaim to you: what was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and our hands have touched (concerning the word of life— 2and the life was revealed, and we have seen and testify and announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us).

elements.question: What does John want his readers to know about himself and the other apostles?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at the verbs John uses for how the apostles came to know the word of life.
elements.questionHint: What verbs does John use to describe how the apostles came to know about “the word of life,” and what do those verbs suggest about the kind of knowledge they had?
elements.sampleAnswer: John wants his readers to know that he and the other apostles were direct, physical witnesses to “the word of life” — that is, to Jesus himself. They didn’t receive a vision or a secondhand report; they heard him, saw him with their own eyes, and touched him with their hands. Furthermore, the one they encountered was none other than “the eternal life that was with the Father” — making plain that Jesus is of divine origin. This testimony is therefore both humanly verifiable (eyewitness accounts) and divinely significant (encounter with the pre-existent Son).
elements.mainPoint: The apostles **physically met Jesus**, the eternal life from the Father, so their testimony is both real and divine.

elements.question: How does John describe Jesus? What does that tell us?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the two descriptions John gives of Jesus, and where each says he came from.
elements.questionHint:
What two titles does John give Jesus in these verses?
What do each of them imply about Jesus’s origins and nature?
elements.sampleAnswer: John describes Jesus as “the word of life” (v1) and “the eternal life that was with the Father” (v2). These phrases are remarkable because they identify Jesus not merely as a teacher or prophet, but as the very life of God made visible and tangible. “The word of life” echoes the language of John’s Gospel — a person who is the agent and embodiment of life itself. “The eternal life that was with the Father” goes further still, pointing to Jesus’s pre-existence alongside the Father before the incarnation. This tells us that in encountering Jesus, the apostles encountered nothing less than God’s own life breaking into human history.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus is **the word of life and eternal life itself**, who existed with the Father before he appeared, and so is divine.

elements.passageText: 3What we have seen and heard we announce to you too, so that you may have fellowship with us (and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ). 4Thus we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.

elements.question: What outcomes does John want as he proclaims Jesus to them?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look for the two results John says he wants, one in verse 3 and one in verse 4.
elements.questionHint: What two things does John say he is writing “so that” will happen — and how are those two things related to each other?
elements.sampleAnswer: John states two outcomes. The first is fellowship: he announces what he has seen and heard so that his readers may share in the same fellowship that the apostles have — a fellowship that is ultimately with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ (v3). This is extraordinary: John’s proclamation is the means by which his readers enter into relationship with God himself. The second outcome is complete joy (v4) — John’s own joy, and implicitly his readers’ too. These goals are intimately connected: fellowship with God produces fullness of joy, and John writing the letter is how that fellowship and joy are extended to others.
elements.mainPoint: John wants his readers to share **fellowship with God and his Son**, and so to have complete joy.

elements.question: What implications do the apostles’ fellowship with the Father and Son have for John’s readers?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about whose fellowship the apostles enjoy, and what it means that readers can join in.
elements.questionHint: If the apostles’ fellowship is “with the Father and with his Son,” and John says he is writing so that his readers may “have fellowship with us,” what does that imply about where the readers will ultimately find themselves?
elements.sampleAnswer: The implication is breathtaking: because the apostles have genuine fellowship with the Father and the Son, and because they are announcing what they have seen and heard, those who receive that announcement can share in the very same fellowship. John’s readers don’t need to have been present with Jesus in person — their fellowship with the Father and Son comes through receiving the apostolic testimony. This means the letter itself is the channel of that fellowship, and it means the readers’ standing before God is not inferior to that of the apostles; they are invited into the same relationship.
elements.mainPoint: Readers who receive the apostles’ message share **the same fellowship with the Father and the Son** as the apostles.

elements.question: Why do you think John starts here? Given what we know about the situation of his readers, why is this an important place to start?
elements.questionHintFirst: Picture readers shaken by people who have just left, and ask what firm ground they most need.
elements.questionHint: If your readers are confused about who to trust, what would be the most stabilising thing you could tell them about the source of your message?
elements.sampleAnswer: John’s readers have been shaken by the departure of people who seemed to be confident, authoritative Christians. In that crisis, the most important thing John can do is direct them back to the bedrock: not the opinions of the departing teachers, not their own uncertain feelings, but the concrete, physical, eyewitness testimony of those who were actually there with Jesus. By starting with “what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and our hands have touched,” John is saying: whatever those who left may claim, the foundation of your faith is not their teaching — it is this verifiable, apostolic encounter with the eternal life that was with the Father.
elements.mainPoint: John steadies unsettled readers by pointing them to **the apostles’ eyewitness testimony**, not to the teachers who left.

elements.text: 1:5–2:2: Those who walk in the light are those who take their sin to Jesus

elements.passageText: 5Now this is the gospel message we have heard from him and announce to you: God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all.

elements.question: How does John summarise the apostles’ message?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice how John says the same thing about God in two different ways.
elements.questionHint:
Why do you think John not only says “God is light” but goes on to add “in him there is no darkness at all”?
What does the repetition add?
elements.sampleAnswer: John summarises the apostolic message in a single, absolute statement: “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all.” The doubling of the idea — first positively (“God is light”) and then negatively with an emphatic “at all” (“no darkness at all”) — underlines the absolute purity and holiness of God’s nature. This is not a gentle metaphor about God being nice; it is a declaration that God is morally and spiritually perfect, utterly without shadow or compromise. Everything that follows in the letter flows from this foundational claim about who God is.
elements.mainPoint: John sums up the apostles’ teaching as the **absolute purity and holiness of God**, pictured through light and darkness.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Think again back to John’s Gospel: how are the metaphors of light/darkness used there? What is John saying about God here?

elements.passageText: 6If we say we have fellowship with him and yet keep on walking in the darkness, we are lying and not practicing the truth. 7But if we walk in the light as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin. 8If we say we do not bear the guilt of sin, we are deceiving ourselves and the truth is not in us. 9But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous, forgiving us our sins and cleansing us from all unrighteousness. 10If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar and his word is not in us.

elements.question: We then get three claims about sin. What might people claim (and probably this is exactly what people were claiming!)?
elements.questionHintFirst: Find the three “if we say” statements and note what each one claims.
elements.questionHint:
Look at the three “if we say” statements.
Are they all saying the same thing, or is there a progression or difference between them?
elements.sampleAnswer: The three claims are: (1) “We have fellowship with God” while continuing to walk in darkness (v6) — a claim to spiritual intimacy that is contradicted by a pattern of life that ignores God’s holiness; (2) “We do not bear the guilt of sin” (v8) — a claim to sinlessness in the present, perhaps meaning “we are spiritually enlightened beyond the realm of sin”; and (3) “We have not sinned” (v10) — a more sweeping claim that denies any history of personal sin, which would effectively make God a liar since his word declares all people to be sinners. These were likely the actual claims of the false teachers who had departed.
elements.mainPoint: The claims are **intimacy with God while living in darkness, freedom from sin’s guilt, and never having sinned at all**.

elements.passageText: 1(My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin.) But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the Righteous One, 2and he himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for our sins but also for the whole world.

elements.question: What does John have to say about the people making these claims? What does this tell us about the real relationship that Christians have with sin in this fallen world?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the aim John states at the start of 2:1 and what he adds straight after.
elements.questionHint:
Notice the parenthesis John opens with in 2:1.
What does it tell you about the balance he is trying to strike between taking sin seriously and not despairing when we sin?
elements.sampleAnswer: John’s response to the claimants in 1:6–10 is blunt: they are lying, deceiving themselves, and making God a liar. But in 2:1–2, his tone becomes pastoral and warm (“my little children”). He makes clear that his goal is not that Christians would become complacent about sin, but that they would not sin. Yet he is also realistic: “if anyone does sin” — and the implication is that they will. The remedy is not self-improvement or spiritual superiority, but the advocacy of Jesus Christ the righteous One and his atoning sacrifice. Christians in this fallen world are people who sin but who have a permanent advocate and a fully sufficient atonement.
elements.mainPoint: Christians still sin, but **Jesus is their advocate and the atoning sacrifice**, so there is no room for complacency or despair.

elements.passageText: 7But if we walk in the light as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.

elements.question: Given what John has said about the claims of those who ‘walk in darkness’, what does it mean to ‘walk in the light’?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask whether walking in the light can mean sinlessness, given that cleansing is still needed.
elements.questionHint:
If walking in the light still requires the blood of Jesus to cleanse from sin, what does that tell you about what “walking in the light” actually means?
Is it about being sinless?
elements.sampleAnswer: Walking in the light is the opposite of the false claims John has just exposed. It does not mean achieving sinlessness — note that even those who walk in the light still need the blood of Jesus to cleanse them from sin (v7). Rather, walking in the light means living in honest openness before God: acknowledging sin rather than denying it, confessing rather than concealing, and relying on Jesus rather than claiming to be beyond the need of his cleansing. It is a posture of truthfulness and dependence, not a claim to moral perfection.
elements.mainPoint: To walk in the light is to live **honestly before God**, admitting sin and relying on Jesus’s blood, not claiming perfection.

elements.question: What truths does John counter each of the false claims with?
elements.questionHintFirst: For each “if we say” claim, look for what John says in reply.
elements.questionHint: For each “if we say” claim in v6, v8, and v10, can you find the corresponding “but if” or corrective statement that John gives in response?
elements.sampleAnswer: To the claim “we have fellowship with God while walking in darkness” (v6), John counters that walking in the light brings real fellowship and real cleansing through Jesus’s blood (v7). To the claim “we do not bear the guilt of sin” (v8), he counters that confessing sins brings faithful forgiveness and cleansing from God (v9). To the claim “we have not sinned” (v10), he counters that denying sin makes God himself a liar, since his word declares otherwise. In each case, the counter-truth either exposes the claim as self-deception or points to Jesus as the real solution to the sin the claimants are denying.
elements.mainPoint: John answers each claim with **Jesus’s cleansing and God’s forgiveness**, or exposes it as self-deception that makes God a liar.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: What is the overarching truth that unites John’s counterargument?

elements.text: 2:3–11: Real knowledge of God leads to love for your brothers and sisters

elements.passageText:
3Now by this we know that we have come to know God: if we keep his commandments. 4The one who says “I have come to know God” and yet does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in such a person. 5But whoever obeys his word, truly in this person the love of God has been perfected. By this we know that we are in him. 6The one who says he resides in God ought himself to walk just as Jesus walked.

7Dear friends, I am not writing a new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you have had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have already heard. 8On the other hand, I am writing a new commandment to you which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining. 9The one who says he is in the light but still hates his fellow Christian is still in the darkness. 10The one who loves his fellow Christian resides in the light, and there is no cause for stumbling in him. 11But the one who hates his fellow Christian is in the darkness, walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.

elements.question: We now get another three claims (‘whoever says/claims’). What are these claims, what shows they are false, and what theme unites them?
elements.questionHintFirst: Find the three “whoever says” claims, and the common test John applies to each.
elements.questionHint:
What is the one thing John keeps returning to as the practical test of whether a spiritual claim is genuine?
Can you trace it through all three claims?
elements.sampleAnswer: The three claims are: (1) “I have come to know God” — exposed as false by not keeping his commandments (v4); (2) “I reside in God” — exposed as false by not walking as Jesus walked (v6); (3) “I am in the light” — exposed as false by hating a fellow Christian (v9). The theme uniting all three is that genuine knowledge of God, genuine indwelling in God, and genuine standing in the light cannot be separated from obedience and from love for God’s people. The false teachers were apparently making impressive spiritual claims while living in a way that contradicted those claims. For John, claims about relationship with God without the corresponding ethical and relational fruit are simply lies.
elements.mainPoint: Claims to know God, to remain in him and to be in the light are proved false without **obedience and love for fellow believers**.

elements.passageText: 9The one who says he is in the light but still hates his fellow Christian is still in the darkness. 10The one who loves his fellow Christian resides in the light, and there is no cause for stumbling in him. 11But the one who hates his fellow Christian is in the darkness, walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.

elements.question: What does John have to say about the people making these claims?
elements.questionHintFirst: Compare verse 9 with verse 11 and notice what John adds the second time.
elements.questionHint:
Compare what John says about the person who hates in v9 with what he says in v11.
Does he simply repeat himself, or does he add something further?
elements.sampleAnswer: John is stark: the person who claims to be in the light while hating a fellow Christian “is still in the darkness” (v9). They are not partially in the light and partially in the dark — they are still entirely in the darkness. And v11 deepens this: the one who hates a fellow Christian not only is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, but “does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.” The implication is serious — this is not a minor inconsistency but a fundamental disorientation. They cannot see clearly because they have chosen darkness, and that blindness affects their whole direction.
elements.mainPoint: Hating a fellow believer shows someone is wholly in the darkness, left **disoriented and spiritually blind**.

elements.passageText: 7Dear friends, I am not writing a new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you have had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have already heard. 8On the other hand, I am writing a new commandment to you which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.

elements.question: What does it look like to obey ‘the command’ of God here?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the two words John uses to describe this commandment, and ask in what sense each one is true.
elements.questionHint:
John calls it both old and new: what makes it old, and what makes it new?
Read on into verses 9–11 to see what sort of behaviour shows someone is obeying it.
elements.sampleAnswer: John is not announcing a fresh rule. The command is the old one his readers have had from the beginning, the message they first heard. It is also new in the sense that it is now being truly lived out “in him and in you”, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining. Obeying it therefore means living by that original message in the light of Christ, and the verses that follow show the practical test: loving fellow Christians instead of hating them.
elements.mainPoint: The command is **the original message** from the beginning, now lived out afresh in Christ as the darkness fades, and the next verses show it means loving fellow believers.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: What do v7–8 sound like? How does that and the context help us understand what the disobedience of God looked like here?

elements.question: What three counterarguments does John give to these claims?
elements.questionHintFirst: John answers in three steps across the three verses: one negative, one positive, one further negative.
elements.questionHint:
John gives a negative, a positive, and then a further negative response across v9–11.
What does each one add to his overall case against the false claimants?
elements.sampleAnswer: The three counterarguments are: (1) Whoever claims to be in the light but hates their fellow Christian is in fact “still in the darkness” — the claim is directly falsified (v9); (2) Conversely, the one who loves their fellow Christian genuinely “resides in the light,” and there is no cause for stumbling in them — love is the positive proof of what the claimants say they have (v10); (3) The one who hates is not only in the darkness but walks in it and doesn’t know where they’re going, because the darkness has blinded them (v11) — so the false claimant is not only wrong but dangerously disoriented. Together, these amount to a devastating exposure: the claims prove nothing; behaviour reveals everything.
elements.mainPoint: Hatred leaves a person in darkness, love **proves they live in the light**, and hatred ends in blindness.

elements.passageText: 13I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life.

elements.question: Given the fact that it is clear from 1 John that some perhaps seemingly impressive Christians have abandoned the apostles’ teaching, how would this passage have reassured John’s readers (remember the aim in 5:13) and exposed what was really going on?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about what “know” means for readers who may be doubting after others have left.
elements.questionHint:
If John’s purpose is that his readers “may know” they have eternal life, what role do the tests in chapters 1–2 play?
Do they create doubt, or do they settle it?
elements.sampleAnswer: John’s stated purpose in 5:13 is that believers may “know” — with certainty — that they have eternal life. The tests in the early chapters of the letter serve this double purpose. For the genuine believers, they are reassuring: if you walk in the light, confess your sins, keep God’s commands, and love your fellow Christians, then you have the marks of someone who truly knows God. You don’t need to be intimidated by those who left; their departure and their loveless lives expose them rather than condemn you. For the departing teachers, the same tests function as an exposure: their claimed spiritual superiority is undermined by the very lack of love and obedience that John says characterises a genuine relationship with God.
elements.mainPoint: The tests in the letter **give believers certainty** that they have eternal life, while exposing the teachers who left.

elements.text: Application

elements.question: What does 1 John have to say to those who say ‘I like Jesus but I don’t much like Paul, John, etc.’?
As we experience the ongoing reality of sin in this fallen world, how can this passage reassure us that we have eternal life?

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: How does this passage help us not to despair at the state of our own hearts?

elements.question: How can we use this passage to help each other ‘walk just as Jesus walked’?

deeper.question: What will it look like for us to obey God?

elements.text:
Last time we saw that John begins by establishing the apostolic testimony as the sure foundation for his readers’ faith. He then confronted a series of false claims — about sin, about knowing God, about love — and in each case pointed his readers back to the truth. The result was both an exposure of what was false and a reassurance for those who were genuinely walking with God.

Before we dive in today, take a moment to recap: what did we learn about sin and love last time? What did that imply about the false teachers John was warning against? And how was it reassuring for those who remained? (Think about John’s aim in 5:13.)

elements.question: It’s worth reading the whole passage before you begin…

elements.text: 2:12–14: This is why I am writing

elements.passageText: 12I am writing to you, little children, that your sins have been forgiven because of his name. 13I am writing to you, fathers, that you have known him who has been from the beginning. I am writing to you, young people, that you have conquered the evil one. 14I have written to you, children, that you have known the Father. I have written to you, fathers, that you have known him who has been from the beginning. I have written to you, young people, that you are strong, and the word of God resides in you, and you have conquered the evil one.

elements.question: Take a moment in twos or threes to look at 2:12–14. What do you notice? What repetition is there? What differences are there?
elements.questionHintFirst: Count the groups John names and compare the two rounds of addressing them.
elements.questionHint:
Look at what John says about each group.
Are these things he is urging them to achieve, or things he is telling them they already have?
elements.sampleAnswer: The most obvious feature is the rhythmic repetition: John addresses three groups — “little children,” “fathers,” and “young people” — twice, first with “I am writing to you” and then with “I have written to you.” The repetition for “fathers” is almost identical in both rounds, while for “little children/children” and “young people” there are slight additions in the second round. The things John affirms about each group are striking: forgiveness of sins and knowledge of the Father for the children; knowledge of the one “from the beginning” for the fathers; conquest of the evil one and strength and the word dwelling in them for the young people. It is a remarkable list of confident assurances — not commands, but declarations of what is already true.
elements.mainPoint: John addresses **children, fathers and young people twice**, affirming what is already true of them rather than commanding.

elements.question: How do these verses pick up on what we have already seen so far?
elements.questionHintFirst: Match each thing John affirms here with a theme from chapters 1 and 2.
elements.questionHint: Can you match each thing John affirms about his readers in v12–14 to something he has already said earlier in the letter?
elements.sampleAnswer: These verses gather up several of the key themes from 1:1–2:11. Forgiveness of sins (v12) picks up the promise of 1:9 — confession brings forgiveness — and the advocacy of 2:1–2. Knowledge of God and the Father (v13–14) echoes 2:3–6, where John said the test of knowing God is keeping his commands. Conquering the evil one and having the word of God reside in them (v14) picks up the light/darkness framework of chapters 1–2, in which those who walk in the light have overcome the false claims. Whereas the preceding verses have been largely polemical (exposing false claims), here John pauses to affirm what is already true of his readers — as a basis for what he is about to say.
elements.mainPoint: John gathers up earlier themes, **forgiveness, knowing God and overcoming evil**, to assure readers of what they already have.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Remember that John is writing to reassure the believers that they have eternal life (5:13). Based on what we have seen in the letter so far, how is he doing that here?

elements.text: 2:15–17: Do not love this passing world

elements.passageText: 15Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him,

elements.question: John sets out a very stark choice in v15. What is it?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice whether John says loving the world weakens love for the Father, or something stronger.
elements.questionHint:
John doesn’t say loving the world weakens your love for the Father — he says the love of the Father is simply “not in” the person who loves the world.
What does that absoluteness imply?
elements.sampleAnswer: The choice is absolute: you either love the world, or you have the love of the Father in you — you cannot have both. John frames this as a mutually exclusive either/or: “if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” There is no middle ground or partial loyalty available. The world and the Father represent two entirely different sources and objects of allegiance, and they are incompatible. This stark framing is characteristic of John’s writing and is designed to force a clear-eyed reckoning with where one’s true loyalty lies.
elements.mainPoint: It is a **stark either/or**: a person cannot love the world and also have the Father’s love.

elements.question: What does it mean to love the world?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at the three things John says make up what is “in the world” in verse 16.
elements.questionHint: How does John define the content of “the world” in v16 — and do any of those three categories feel recognisable in your own culture?
elements.sampleAnswer: John defines the world’s content in v16: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the arrogance produced by material possessions. Loving the world therefore means setting your heart on what the world offers — physical gratification, the allure of what you see and want, and the pride that comes from what you own or achieve. Crucially, John says these things are “not from the Father, but is from the world” — they have a different origin and a different end. Loving the world is not simply enjoying physical things; it is allowing these cravings to define your identity, direct your choices, and claim your ultimate loyalty.
elements.mainPoint: Loving the world means letting **cravings, covetous looking and pride in possessions** rule the heart.

elements.passageText: 15Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, 16because all that is in the world (the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and the arrogance produced by material possessions) is not from the Father, but is from the world. 17And the world is passing away with all its desires, but the person who does the will of God remains forever.

elements.question: What reasons does John give for not loving the world?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at verse 16 for where these things come from, and verse 17 for where they are heading.
elements.questionHint: What contrast does John draw in v17 between the world and the person who does God’s will — and what does that contrast suggest about the wisest investment of our love?
elements.sampleAnswer: John gives two reasons. The first is about origin: everything in the world — the desires and the arrogance — is not from the Father but from the world (v16). Loving the world therefore means aligning yourself with something that has nothing to do with God. The second reason is about destiny: the world and its desires are passing away (v17). They are temporary, fading, and ultimately doomed. By contrast, the person who does the will of God “remains forever.” The contrast is between the transient and the eternal — and it makes loving the world not just wrong but foolish, since you would be investing yourself in something that will not last.
elements.mainPoint: The world is **opposed to God in origin and temporary in destiny**, whereas whoever obeys God lasts for ever.

elements.passageText: 8On the other hand, I am writing a new commandment to you which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.

elements.question: In 2:8, we were told that the darkness was passing. What was the darkness here and what did it mean for it to pass?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at the verses either side of 2:8 to see what kind of darkness John has in mind.
elements.questionHint: Given the verses immediately around v8, what kind of behaviour does John associate with “darkness,” and what new reality is making that darkness fade?
elements.sampleAnswer: In the context of 2:7–11, the “darkness” is most immediately the darkness of hatred — specifically, of hating one’s fellow Christian. The “new commandment” is the commandment of love, and John says the darkness of a world without this love is already beginning to pass because “the true light is already shining” — a reference to the coming of Jesus, whose life and love have inaugurated a new era. The passing of the darkness means that the old order of hostility and division is being displaced by the light of Christ’s love, which now shines in those who belong to him. This connects to 2:17 where the world itself is “passing away” — both point to the same eschatological shift.
elements.mainPoint: The darkness of **hatred and loveless living is fading** because Christ’s coming has begun a new age of love.

elements.text: 2:18–27: Antichrists deny the truth about Jesus, but you know it

elements.passageText: 18Children, it is the last hour, and just as you heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. We know from this that it is the last hour. 19They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us, because if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us. But they went out from us to demonstrate that all of them do not belong to us.

elements.question: Now we see the reality of the world as it passes away — ‘last hour’. How do John’s readers know it is the last hour?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at what John says his readers already know, and what has now happened to confirm it.
elements.questionHint: What is the connection John draws between the appearance of “many antichrists” and the claim that it is “the last hour”?
elements.sampleAnswer: John says they know it is the last hour because of the appearance of “many antichrists.” His readers had already been taught that “the antichrist is coming” — apparently an expected end-times figure. The fact that many antichrists have now appeared is for John a sign that the last hour has already begun. The departure of these people from the community (v19) is itself evidence: those who leave and oppose the apostolic truth about Jesus are the manifestation of the antichrist spirit that signals the end times are underway. The crisis in the church is not just a pastoral problem — it is an eschatological marker.
elements.mainPoint: The arrival of **many antichrists** shows the last hour has already begun.

elements.passageText: 18Children, it is the last hour, and just as you heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. We know from this that it is the last hour.

elements.question: What comes to mind when you hear the word ‘antichrist’? What do we learn here?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice where John says the antichrists went out from.
elements.questionHint: If John says antichrists “went out from us” — that is, from the church — what does that tell us about where the antichrist threat actually comes from?
elements.sampleAnswer: Many people think of “antichrist” in terms of dramatic future evil — a single, world-dominating figure associated with the end of the world, as depicted in popular culture. What John says here is both more surprising and more sobering: many antichrists have already appeared, and they came from within the church community. “Antichrist” doesn’t mean overtly demonic or obviously sinister — these were people who seemed to belong to the Christian fellowship. The defining characteristic, unpacked in v22, is that they deny that Jesus is the Christ. An antichrist is therefore anyone who offers an alternative to the true Jesus, however respectable their appearance.
elements.mainPoint: Antichrists are **people from within the church** who deny Jesus, not just a future world ruler.

elements.passageText: 19They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us, because if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us. But they went out from us to demonstrate that all of them do not belong to us.

elements.question: Look at the repetition of ‘us’ in v19 and compare it with 1:1–4. Who is ‘us’? What does the repetition of ‘us’ in v19 tell us about the antichrists?
elements.questionHintFirst: Watch how often John uses “us” in verse 19 and what he says departure proves.
elements.questionHint:
John says the antichrists’ departure “demonstrates” something.
What exactly does it demonstrate?
Why is that logically significant?
elements.sampleAnswer: In 1:1–4, “us” referred to the apostolic circle — those who personally witnessed and handled the word of life. In 2:19, the “us” is the community of genuine believers centred on that apostolic testimony. The repetition of “went out from us … did not belong to us … remained with us … went out from us … do not belong to us” is striking for its insistence: these people were in the fellowship outwardly, but their departure demonstrates that they never truly belonged. The test of genuine belonging is not impressive claims or confident teaching — it is remaining with the apostolic community and its teaching. Departure exposes that the root was never there.
elements.mainPoint: Leaving **proves they never truly belonged** to the genuine community built on the apostles’ teaching.

elements.passageText:
20Nevertheless you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you all know. 21I have not written to you that you do not know the truth, but that you do know it, and that no lie is of the truth. 22Who is the liar but the person who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This one is the antichrist: the person who denies the Father and the Son. 23Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either. The person who confesses the Son has the Father also.

24As for you, what you have heard from the beginning must remain in you. If what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father. 25Now this is the promise that he himself made to us: eternal life. 26These things I have written to you about those who are trying to deceive you.

27Now as for you, the anointing that you received from him resides in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about all things, it is true and is not a lie. Just as it has taught you, you reside in him.

elements.question: How does John reassure his readers by pointing out how they are different from the antichrists?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look for what John says his readers have received that the antichrists lack.
elements.questionHint: What does John say his readers have that the antichrists apparently lack — and how does that resource protect them?
elements.sampleAnswer: John makes a sharp contrast between the antichrists and his readers. The antichrists have gone out and are spreading deception (v26). But his readers have an anointing from the Holy One — the Spirit himself — and because of this anointing, they already know the truth (v20–21). They don’t need the antichrists to teach them, because the anointing they received from God teaches them about all things and is entirely reliable (v27). Furthermore, the original message they received — “what you have heard from the beginning” — is itself the antidote: if they remain in it, they remain in the Son and in the Father (v24), and the result is the promise of eternal life (v25). The readers’ advantage over the antichrists is not superior intelligence but the Spirit’s indwelling and the foundational gospel message.
elements.mainPoint: Readers are **protected by the Spirit’s anointing** and by holding to the gospel they first received.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Note the repetition of ‘anointing’ in v20–27. [Perhaps the antichrists themselves claimed to have superior ‘anointing’ just as they perhaps claimed superior sinlessness and superior knowledge of God.]

elements.passageText: 22Who is the liar but the person who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This one is the antichrist: the person who denies the Father and the Son. 23Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either. The person who confesses the Son has the Father also.

elements.question: How does John further expose the antichrists as offering an alternative gospel?
elements.questionHintFirst: Follow the logic of verse 23 about the Father and the Son.
elements.questionHint: What does the logic of v23 imply about anyone who claims to know and love “God” while rejecting or redefining who Jesus is?
elements.sampleAnswer: John identifies the antichrists’ lie precisely: they deny that Jesus is the Christ (v22). This is not simply a doctrinal detail — it has radical consequences. Because the Father and the Son are inseparably related, denying the Son means losing the Father too (v23). Any religion or teaching that offers “God” while denying that Jesus is the Christ is therefore not a different route to the same destination — it is a lie that cuts people off from the Father entirely. The antichrists may have claimed to offer something more spiritual or sophisticated, but John’s logic is unsparing: deny the Son, lose the Father. Confess the Son, and you have the Father also.
elements.mainPoint: To reject Jesus as Messiah is **to lose God altogether**, because Father and Son cannot be separated.

elements.passageText: 24As for you, what you have heard from the beginning must remain in you. If what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father. 25Now this is the promise that he himself made to us: eternal life.

elements.question: What is the antidote to antichrists?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice that John points back to something old rather than offering something new.
elements.questionHint:
Notice that John says “what you heard from the beginning” — not “something new I’m telling you.”
What does that suggest about where the protection against false teaching comes from?
elements.sampleAnswer: The antidote is simple but demanding: let what you heard from the beginning remain in you (v24). John does not call his readers to find something new to counteract the antichrists, but to hold on to what they have already received — the original apostolic gospel about Jesus. The logic is equally simple: if the original message remains in them, they remain in the Son and in the Father, and the consequence of that is the promised eternal life (v25). The antichrists are offering novelty and supposed spiritual advancement; John’s counter is not a more sophisticated argument but a return to the foundation. Against false teaching, the antidote is deep rootedness in the true gospel.
elements.mainPoint: The antidote is to **keep holding the original apostolic gospel**, which brings life with the Son and the Father.

elements.question: False teachers seldom wear a T-shirt declaring themselves to be an antichrist. They seldom openly deny Jesus, so they can be very unsettling. What are some ways we can spot a counterfeit gospel that offers an alternative to Jesus and the apostolic message, and how can we help each other remain in the gospel we have heard from the beginning?

elements.text:
There are few things more unsettling than confident, seemingly authoritative teaching that contradicts what you thought you believed. Imagine being in John’s church — people you respected have walked out, and they are now teaching something different. You begin to wonder: who is right? Am I the one who is wrong?

That’s the background to this passage. John is going to talk about sin and the Christian life — but he has a pastoral aim: to keep his readers from being led astray. Before we look at the text, it’s worth asking: what kind of things do people teach about sin and the Christian life today? What about sanctification? How can we tell if such teaching is wrong?

elements.question: What enables the children of God to ‘remain in him’ in contrast to those who have departed (2:19)?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask what John says is teaching them, and whether the reason is their own effort.
elements.questionHint:
What does John point to as the reason his readers can remain in God?
Is it their own determination, or something else entirely?
elements.sampleAnswer: What enables them to remain is the anointing from God — the Spirit — who resides in them. Unlike the antichrists who “went out from us” (2:19), the genuine children of God have an internal resource that keeps them: the Spirit’s teaching, which is true and not a lie. The contrast is sharp: the antichrists departed because they had no real root; the believers remain because the Spirit dwells within them and continually teaches them the truth. Remaining in God is not therefore an achievement of human willpower but the outworking of a divine indwelling.
elements.mainPoint: The Spirit’s **anointing** teaches believers the truth and keeps them in Christ, which is God’s work and not human willpower.

elements.passageText: 28And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink away from him in shame when he comes back.

elements.question: In response to this truth then, what command does John give his readers in 2:28 and why?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at what John says may happen “when he appears”.
elements.questionHint: What does John say will happen “when he appears” — and how does that future prospect motivate the present command to remain?
elements.sampleAnswer: The command is “remain in him.” The reason John gives is forward-looking and personal: so that when Jesus appears (at his return), his readers will have confidence before him and will not shrink away in shame. This is a striking motivation — not primarily a matter of present comfort or current performance, but a future encounter with Jesus himself. John wants his readers to be people who, when they stand before Jesus at his coming, will not be ashamed of how they have lived. The command is grounded in assurance (you have the Spirit and the truth), not in anxiety.
elements.mainPoint: Believers are told to **remain in Christ** now so that they can meet him at his return with confidence, not shame.

elements.passageText: 29If you know that he is righteous, you also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been fathered by him.

elements.question: Remember that the wider context here (indeed the whole letter) is about ‘antichrists’ and how to avoid being led astray by them (3:7). How does ‘family resemblance to God’ in v29 help us here, both positively and negatively?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about what children of a righteous father are like.
elements.questionHint: If children resemble their parents, what should you expect to see in the life of someone who has genuinely been “fathered by” a righteous God?
elements.sampleAnswer: Verse 29 introduces the family resemblance principle: because God is righteous, those who have been born of him practice righteousness. This works positively and negatively. Positively, it gives John’s readers a way to recognise genuine children of God — including themselves: the practice of righteousness is a mark of genuine new birth, not a performance to earn acceptance. Negatively, it exposes the antichrists: their departure and their failure to practice righteousness and love reveals that they were never born of God, regardless of how impressive their claims. The test cuts both ways — confirming the genuine and exposing the false.
elements.mainPoint: Those born of the righteous God **resemble him by practising righteousness**, which marks genuine believers and exposes counterfeits.

elements.question: How does John avoid his readers falling into despair by worrying that they aren’t ‘righteous enough’?
elements.questionHintFirst: Compare what is already true of believers now with what has not yet been revealed.
elements.questionHint:
Notice that John says “we are God’s children now” and “what we will be has not yet been revealed”.
What does the gap between those two things tell us about where Christians currently stand?
elements.sampleAnswer: John heads off despair by grounding his readers’ identity not in their current performance but in what the Father has already done: they are called God’s children — “and indeed we are!” (v1). This is present-tense reality, not a future achievement. But he also introduces a crucial forward dimension: what they will be has not yet been revealed (v2). They are God’s children now, but their full transformation is still to come — when Jesus is revealed, they will be like him because they will see him as he is. This means the standard is not “perfect righteousness now” but “ongoing hope directed towards him,” which produces present purification (v3). The pressure of impossible current perfection is relieved by the promise of future transformation.
elements.mainPoint: Believers **already are God’s children** and will be fully transformed when Jesus appears, so hope replaces despair.

elements.question: What implications do these truths have for how the believer relates to the world and how they grow as Christians?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at how the world responded to Jesus, and at what hope does to us in verse 3.
elements.questionHint: What does John say in v3 is the motivating force for personal purification — and how is that different from trying to be good out of fear or duty?
elements.sampleAnswer: The implications are twofold. In relation to the world: the world doesn’t recognise God’s children, just as it didn’t recognise Jesus (v1). This means believers should not be surprised or destabilised by the world’s incomprehension or hostility — it is a consequence of belonging to a different family. In relation to growth: the hope of seeing Jesus and being like him is itself a purifying power (v3). Christian growth is not primarily driven by guilt or law but by a future-orientated hope — the more clearly we hold on to the prospect of seeing Jesus as he is, the more we are drawn to live in a way that is consistent with that hope and his purity.
elements.mainPoint: The world will not understand God’s children, but **the hope of seeing Jesus** purifies them from within.

elements.question: Before we look at the details of this section, what clues are there as to John’s pastoral purpose in writing it?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look for a direct warning in verse 7 and ask what it suggests someone was doing.
elements.questionHint: Is there a phrase in v7 where John directly names what he is trying to prevent — and what does that tell you about what the false teachers may have been saying?
elements.sampleAnswer: The most explicit clue is v7: “little children, let no one deceive you.” John’s direct address and warning about deception tells us that someone is actively trying to mislead his readers about exactly this topic — the relationship between righteousness, sin, and belonging to God. The false teachers who have departed may have been teaching that sin doesn’t matter, or that their spiritual status placed them beyond ordinary moral categories. John’s pastoral purpose is to defend his readers against that deception by giving them a clear, theologically robust account of how sin and righteousness relate to genuine Christian identity.
elements.mainPoint: John’s warning that **no one should deceive** his readers shows that false teachers were misleading them about sin and righteousness.

elements.passageText: 4Everyone who practices sin also practices lawlessness; indeed, sin is lawlessness. 5And you know that Jesus was revealed to take away sins, and in him there is no sin. 6Everyone who resides in him does not sin; everyone who sins has neither seen him nor known him.

elements.question: Can you see any difficulties with these verses in the light of what we have already seen in 1 John? How are we to understand them?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at the verb forms John uses and ask whether he means every single act.
elements.questionHint: Does John use the word “practice” or “practices” in these verses — and if so, what does that suggest about the kind of sin he has in mind?
elements.sampleAnswer: The difficulty is obvious: if “everyone who resides in him does not sin” (v6) and “everyone who has been fathered by God does not practice sin” (v9), how does this square with 1:8 — “if we say we do not bear the guilt of sin, we are deceiving ourselves”? The key is the Greek verb tenses and the use of “practice.” John is using present continuous tense — the language of persistent, habitual pattern of life, not of individual acts. He is not saying Christians never commit individual sins (1:8–9 makes that clear), but that the person who is genuinely born of God will not have sin as the settled, characteristic direction of their life. The contrast is between a life oriented towards righteousness and a life defined by ongoing lawlessness.
elements.mainPoint: John speaks of **habitual practice, not single acts**, so he does not contradict 1:8: believers still sin, but not as a settled way of life.

elements.question: Look at how John continues in v4–10. What is he doing here?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask what John is helping readers to tell apart by the end of verse 10.
elements.questionHint: How does John’s definition of sin in v4 as “lawlessness” connect to his argument that sin is incompatible with belonging to God?
elements.sampleAnswer: John is constructing a comprehensive case that sin and righteousness reveal whose family you belong to. He defines sin as lawlessness (v4), grounding it in a departure from God’s order rather than in merely breaking rules. He then establishes Jesus’s purpose: he was revealed to take away sins and to destroy the devil’s works (v5, 8) — which means a casual attitude to sin is actually inconsistent with what Jesus came to do. He draws out the implication: a person who genuinely resides in Jesus (born of God, with God’s seed in them) will not live in ongoing sin, because their new nature is incompatible with it. And in v10 he brings it to a head: you can tell the children of God from the children of the devil by whether they practice righteousness and love their fellow Christians.
elements.mainPoint: John argues that **sin and righteousness reveal whose family** you belong to, God’s or the devil’s.

elements.question: Looking at this passage as a whole, how would you encourage a believer who is aware of their sin but is worried that this passage means they are not really a Christian after all?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about whether someone troubled by their sin looks like the people John describes.
elements.questionHint: Does the fact that someone is troubled and worried by their sin suggest they are practicing sin as a settled way of life, or something different?
elements.sampleAnswer: The first thing to say is that awareness and distress about sin is itself a mark of a genuine child of God — those who practice sin as a way of life, as the false teachers apparently did, are not troubled by it at all. elements.question: How does this passage naturally connect to what has gone before?
elements.questionHintFirst: Reread the last phrase of 3:10 and see which topic it introduces.
elements.questionHint:
Look back at the end of 3:10.
How does the very last phrase there set up the topic of this entire passage?
elements.sampleAnswer: The connections are numerous. The “children of the devil” theme from 3:10 is immediately illustrated by Cain (v12), who was “of the evil one.” The contrast between the children of God and the children of the devil (3:10) maps directly onto the contrast between those who love and those who hate in this passage. The principle that sin reveals whose family you belong to (3:4–10) is now applied to love: hate is the mark of the devil’s family (Cain), love is the mark of God’s family. The warning against false teaching and the spirit of antichrist (4:1–3) continues the thread from 2:18–27. And the reassurance of 3:19–22 picks up the pastoral concern of 2:28 — that believers should have confidence before God rather than shame.
elements.mainPoint: The passage **develops the contrast between God’s children and the devil’s** by applying it to love and to testing teaching.

elements.passageText: 11For this is the gospel message that you have heard from the beginning: that we should love one another,

elements.question: What does John mean by ‘the gospel message that you have heard from the beginning’?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice where else John has said “from the beginning” and what that signals.
elements.questionHint:
John uses the phrase “from the beginning” several times in this letter.
What does that phrase signal about the authority and age of the message he is referring to?
elements.sampleAnswer: “The message from the beginning” is the original apostolic gospel that John’s readers received when they first became Christians — the same gospel grounded in the apostles’ eyewitness testimony that John established in 1:1–4. In 2:7, the same phrase referred to “the word that you have already heard,” and in 2:24 John urged his readers to let “what you heard from the beginning” remain in them. Here the specific content given is the command to love one another. This is striking: love for fellow believers is not an afterthought to the gospel, it is presented as part of the original message itself, on a par with faith in Jesus.
elements.mainPoint: The original gospel includes **the command to love one another**, as part of the apostles’ message and not an extra.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Where have we seen this phrase before? What was the message last time? What is it this time?

elements.passageText: 12not like Cain who was of the evil one and brutally murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his deeds were evil, but his brother’s were righteous.

elements.question: What does John say about Cain? (v12) How does this connect to what has gone before?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask what John says Cain’s deeds and Abel’s deeds were like.
elements.questionHint:
What reason does John give for why Cain murdered Abel?
How does that reason illuminate the hostility that John’s readers are experiencing from the world?
elements.sampleAnswer: John identifies Cain as belonging to “the evil one” — the devil himself. This connects directly back to 3:8, where the one who practices sin “is of the devil,” and to 3:10, where those who don’t practice righteousness and don’t love their fellow Christians are revealed as “children of the devil.” Cain’s murder of Abel was not simply a personal crime; it was an act of spiritual enmity, driven by the hatred the evil one’s family has towards those whose deeds are righteous. The reason John gives for the murder is telling: Cain hated Abel because Abel’s deeds were righteous, and that righteousness was intolerable to someone whose deeds were evil. This explains v13: “do not be surprised, brothers and sisters, if the world hates you.”
elements.mainPoint: Cain acted as the devil’s child, **killing out of hatred for goodness**, which explains why the world opposes believers.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Why did John want his readers to be able to distinguish between ‘the children of God’ and the ‘children of the devil’?

elements.passageText: 13Therefore do not be surprised, brothers and sisters, if the world hates you. 14We know that we have crossed over from death to life because we love our fellow Christians. The one who does not love remains in death. 15Everyone who hates his fellow Christian is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life residing in him.

elements.question: What is the significance of v13? And how do v14–15 connect to it? Who is ‘the world’?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask how the world’s hatred and the believers’ love can point in the same direction.
elements.questionHint:
John says both that the world hating you and that you loving fellow Christians point to the same thing.
What is it?
Why do both signs point in the same direction?
elements.sampleAnswer: Verse 13 is significant because it reframes the world’s hostility as something to be expected, not feared: “do not be surprised.” The Cain story explains why — the evil one’s family hates the righteous. “The world” here refers to the system of human life organised apart from and in opposition to God — and by extension those who belong to it, including the antichrists who have departed. Verses 14–15 then turn this on its head: while the world’s hatred is evidence that John’s readers belong to God, their own love for fellow Christians is the positive assurance that they have “crossed over from death to life.” Hate is the mark of death; love is the mark of life. And v15 draws the stark implication: hatred is murder at the level of the heart, and murder is incompatible with eternal life.
elements.mainPoint: The world’s hatred of believers is expected, and **their love for Christians proves they have passed from death to life**.
