elements.question: It’s easy for us to worry that we don’t love our fellow believers enough (sometimes they are genuinely annoying!). How does John help his readers understand what it means to love our brothers and sisters?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at the everyday example in verse 17 that makes the standard of verse 16 concrete.
elements.questionHint: How does the everyday example in v17 help translate the high standard of v16 into something concrete and recognisable in daily life?
elements.sampleAnswer: John grounds love in a specific, observable act: Jesus laying down his life for us (v16). Love is not primarily a feeling — it is a willingness to give up what is yours for the sake of someone else. He then immediately scales this down to an everyday example in v17: if you have material resources and see a fellow Christian in need, closing your heart to them is a failure of love that raises a serious question about whether the love of God is really in you. And v18 makes the practical criterion clear: love that consists only of warm words is not enough; it must be expressed in deeds and in truth. So the standard is not “do I feel warmly enough?” but “am I actually doing something for my brother or sister when they need it?”
elements.mainPoint: Love is **costly action for people in need**, modelled on Christ’s sacrifice, not just warm words or feelings.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: How is this different from what we might feel about them? What might this look like in practice? By contrast, what might hating our brothers and sisters look like in practice?

elements.passageText: 19And by this we will know that we are of the truth and will convince our conscience in his presence, 20that if our conscience condemns us, that God is greater than our conscience and knows all things.

elements.question: John is writing to reassure his readers (5:13). What need for reassurance does he anticipate in v19–20 and how does he go about giving it? Why might our conscience condemn us?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about whether “God is greater than our conscience” is meant to alarm or to comfort.
elements.questionHint:
What does John mean when he says “God is greater than our conscience and knows all things”?
Is that meant to frighten us, or to comfort us?
elements.sampleAnswer: John anticipates that his readers’ own consciences may condemn them — they may feel that their love for fellow Christians has not been sufficient, or that their failures disqualify them. The reassurance he offers is striking: even if our conscience condemns us, God is greater than our conscience and knows all things (v20). This doesn’t mean our conscience is irrelevant or that sin doesn’t matter; it means that God’s knowledge is more comprehensive and his assessment more reliable than our own self-evaluation. If we are genuinely practising love in deed and truth (v18), even imperfectly, we can, in God’s presence, bring our anxious self-judgment before the One whose verdict is the only one that ultimately counts. Our conscience condemns us because we know our failures too well; God knows them — and more — and still forgives.
elements.mainPoint: When conscience accuses us, **God is greater and knows everything**, so we can rest in his judgement and not our own.

elements.passageText: 21Dear friends, if our conscience does not condemn us, we have confidence in the presence of God, 22and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do the things that are pleasing to him.

elements.question: How can we have confidence before God?
elements.questionHintFirst: Trace how a clear conscience, confidence and prayer lead into one another.
elements.questionHint:
What is the connection John draws between having a clear conscience, confidence before God, and effective prayer?
How do these three things flow from one another?
elements.sampleAnswer: John says confidence before God comes when our conscience does not condemn us (v21). This is the positive side of v19–20: when we are living in genuine love, deed, and truth — keeping his commandments and doing what pleases him — we can approach God with openness rather than shame. The result is that prayer becomes confident: “whatever we ask we receive from him” (v22). This is not a guarantee of getting anything we want, but the assurance that a life oriented towards God’s will and characterised by love for others is the context in which prayer is heard and answered. Confidence before God is not the absence of all sin, but the presence of genuine obedience and love as the direction of our lives.
elements.mainPoint: A conscience that does not condemn us, because we love and obey, gives **confidence before God and answered prayer**.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: What does it mean here to ‘keep his commands and do what pleases him’?

elements.text: 4:1–6: But don’t believe everything you’re told

elements.passageText: 1Dear friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to determine if they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.

elements.question: Given what we have picked up about the situation of John’s readers, why do you think he warns them not to ‘believe every spirit’? What reason does John himself give?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the word John uses for how many false prophets there are.
elements.questionHint: Why does John use the word “many” when describing the false prophets — and what does that suggest about the appropriate level of caution his readers should exercise?
elements.sampleAnswer: John’s readers have been confronted by teachers who claimed spiritual authority — people who had been part of their fellowship and were presumably speaking in the name of God or the Spirit. The danger is that impressive spiritual claims could be mistaken for genuine spiritual authority. John’s own reason for the warning is direct: “many false prophets have gone out into the world.” The plural “many” is deliberately alarming — this is not an isolated problem but a widespread one. The existence of false prophets means that spiritual-sounding teaching cannot simply be accepted at face value; it requires testing. The test, however, is not primarily a subjective one about how persuasive or sincere the teacher seems, but an objective one about what they confess about Jesus.
elements.mainPoint: Many false prophets are around, so **spiritual-sounding claims must be tested**, not accepted at face value.

elements.passageText: 2By this you know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses Jesus as the Christ who has come in the flesh is from God, 3but every spirit that refuses to confess Jesus, that spirit is not from God, and this is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming, and now is already in the world.

elements.question: How does John encourage his readers to recognise the Spirit of God (and by implication the spirit of the antichrist)?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at what the spirit must confess about Jesus, and what “in the flesh” adds.
elements.questionHint:
Why do you think John specifies that Jesus “has come in the flesh”?
What would it mean to confess Jesus as the Christ without affirming that he came in the flesh?
elements.sampleAnswer: The test is a specific confessional one: does the spirit (and its teaching) confess that Jesus is the Christ who has come in the flesh (v2)? This criterion is carefully worded — it affirms both the divine identity of Jesus (the Christ, the Son of God) and his genuine physical incarnation (“come in the flesh”). A spirit or teaching that refuses this confession is not from God and carries the antichrist spirit (v3). The test is essentially about whether a teaching presents the full Jesus of the apostolic gospel — both divine and truly human, the Christ who actually became flesh. Any spirituality that separates the divine from the human Jesus, or redefines who he is, fails the test.
elements.mainPoint: A teaching is from God if it **confesses Jesus as the Christ who truly became human**, and otherwise bears the antichrist spirit.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: What might this look like in practice?

elements.passageText: 4You are from God, little children, and have conquered them, because the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world. 5They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world’s perspective and the world listens to them. 6We are from God; the person who knows God listens to us, but whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deceit.

elements.question: What further test does John give in v4–6? Who is ‘us’ here?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at who listens to the apostolic “us” and who does not.
elements.questionHint: Who does John say “the world listens to” versus who it does not listen to — and how does that pattern help identify whether a teaching is from the Spirit of truth or the spirit of deceit?
elements.sampleAnswer: The further test is one of audience: who listens to the teaching? John says those who know God listen to “us” — the apostolic circle — while those who are not from God do not (v6). This is a second diagnostic alongside the confessional test of v2–3. “Us” here, as in 1:1–4, refers to the apostles — the authorised eyewitness witnesses to Jesus. The test is whether a teaching is received by those who genuinely know God and aligned with the apostolic word, or whether it finds its audience primarily among those who are “from the world.” This doesn’t mean popular teaching is wrong, but that teaching which is warmly embraced by the world while contradicting the apostolic gospel is a warning sign.
elements.mainPoint: A second test is **who listens to the apostles’ message**: those who know God do, those of the world do not.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: (Think back to 1:1–4.) What does John mean when he says ‘whoever knows God listens to us’?

elements.question: What encouragement does John leave his readers with in v4–6?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask in what sense the readers “have conquered”, and who makes that possible.
elements.questionHint:
John says his readers “have conquered” the false prophets.
In what sense?
On what basis?
elements.sampleAnswer: The encouragement is bold and personal: “You are from God, little children, and have conquered them” (v4). The conquest is not future — it is already accomplished. The reason is not their own strength or discernment, but the one who is in them: “the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.” God himself, dwelling in his people through his Spirit, is more powerful than the spirit driving the false prophets. John also identifies a second source of confidence in v6: the fact that they receive the apostolic message — “the person who knows God listens to us” — is itself evidence that they are from God. Their responsiveness to the true gospel is a mark of genuine belonging.
elements.mainPoint: Believers have already won because **God in them is greater** than the spirit of the world, and they hear the apostolic message.

elements.text: Application

elements.passageText: 16We have come to know love by this: that Jesus laid down his life for us; thus we ought to lay down our lives for our fellow Christians. 17But whoever has the world’s possessions and sees his fellow Christian in need and shuts off his compassion against him, how can the love of God reside in such a person?

elements.question: Spend some time talking about how we can encourage each other to love like Jesus did by laying down our lives for our brothers and sisters. What is this going to look like in practice? How can we help each other?

elements.passageText: 19And by this we will know that we are of the truth and will convince our conscience in his presence, 20that if our conscience condemns us, that God is greater than our conscience and knows all things. 21Dear friends, if our conscience does not condemn us, we have confidence in the presence of God, 22and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do the things that are pleasing to him.

elements.question: We all know what it is like for our hearts to condemn us. How can this passage encourage us in the knowledge that God is greater than our hearts?

elements.question: How do we help each other test whether a teaching is from God?

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: What might a teaching that denies Jesus look like in practice? How can we encourage each other not to despair about false teaching we encounter?

elements.question: It is important again to remember that there might not be outright denial, but a slight shift away from the centrality of Christ. Does this teaching require something extra from Christians?

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Does it focus on people, leaders, or methodology instead of the cross? Are the teachers characterised by doing what is right and loving the brothers, or not?

elements.text:
‘Love’ is one of the most overused words in the English language. We love our children, we love a good film, we love a particular food. But what does it actually mean? And where does it come from?

In much of our culture, love is primarily understood as a feeling — something that happens to us. John is going to challenge that. For him, love is defined not by how we feel, but by what God has done. And that changes everything.

Before we look at the text, share briefly: how do you think people generally define ‘love’?

elements.question: It’s worth reading the whole passage before you begin…

elements.text: 4:7–21: Love because he first loved us

elements.passageText: 7Dear friends, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves has been fathered by God and knows God. 8The person who does not love does not know God, because God is love.

elements.question: Look at v7–12. ‘Love one another’ appears three times in slightly different ways. What reason is given in v7–8 for the command to love one another?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask where John says love comes from, and what that shows about God himself.
elements.questionHint:
What does John say about where love actually comes from?
What does that tell us about God’s own character?
elements.sampleAnswer: The reason given is that love originates in God himself — it flows from his very nature. Because “God is love” (v8), everyone who has been born of God will love, since they share in his nature. To love is to show that you truly know God; conversely, a failure to love reveals that a person does not know God at all. The command to love one another is therefore grounded not in our feelings or in what others deserve, but in who God is.
elements.mainPoint: Love flows from **God’s own nature**, so those born of him love, and those who do not love do not know him.

elements.passageText:
7Dear friends, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves has been fathered by God and knows God. 8The person who does not love does not know God, because God is love. 9By this the love of God is revealed in us: that God has sent his one and only Son into the world so that we may live through him. 10In this is love: not that we have loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins.

11Dear friends, if God so loved us, then we also ought to love one another. 12No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God resides in us, and his love is perfected in us.

elements.question: How does John define love in these verses (v7–12)? How is that different from the way people talk about love in our society?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at verses 9 and 10 for the specific act that defines love, and who took the first step.
elements.questionHint:
Notice what v10 says about who acted first.
How does that challenge the idea that love is mainly about our own feelings?
elements.sampleAnswer: John defines love by a specific, historical act: God sending his Son as an atoning sacrifice for sins (v9–10). Crucially, he states that the initiative lay entirely with God — “not that we have loved God, but that he loved us” (v10). Love is therefore selfless, sacrificial, and other-directed; it is something God did for us before we deserved it or responded. This is very different from how our culture typically speaks of love, which tends to be emotion-driven (“falling” in love), self-focused (love as a feeling that satisfies us), or conditional (love that can be withdrawn when it’s no longer reciprocated).
elements.mainPoint: True love is seen in God taking **the first step** to give his Son to bear our sins, not in feelings.

elements.question: Taking a step back and looking at all of v7–12, what reasons are given for loving one another?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look for the connecting words, such as “because” and “if”, and list what each gives as a reason.
elements.questionHint:
Can you count the different “because” or “if … then” statements John uses across these verses?
What is each one saying about why we should love?
elements.sampleAnswer: John gives several overlapping reasons. First, love originates in God, so those born of God will naturally love (v7–8). Second, God demonstrated his love concretely by sending his Son so that we might live (v9), and specifically as an atoning sacrifice for sin (v10) — a love entirely initiated by God. Third, because God loved us so extravagantly, we are under an obligation — “we also ought to love one another” (v11). Fourth, loving one another is the way God’s invisible presence becomes visible in the world: since no one can see God, our love for each other is the place where God “resides in us” and his love is brought to completion (v12).
elements.mainPoint: We should love because **love comes from God, he showed it in his Son, and we owe it in return**, making his unseen presence visible.

elements.passageText:
13By this we know that we reside in God and he in us: in that he has given us of his Spirit. 14And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent the Son to be the Savior of the world.

15If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God resides in him and he in God. 16And we have come to know and to believe the love that God has in us. God is love, and the one who resides in love resides in God, and God resides in him.

elements.question: Why do you think this little section is sandwiched between two sections focused on love?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look for what John offers as evidence that God lives in us, then ask how it helps us to love.
elements.questionHint: What three things does John point to in these verses as evidence that God truly lives in us — and how might each of those things give us confidence to love?
elements.sampleAnswer: This section grounds the call to love in the bedrock of Christian assurance. John wants his readers to understand that love isn’t just a moral demand — it flows from an established, indwelling relationship with God. The Spirit’s presence (v13), the apostolic testimony about the Son (v14), and the confession that Jesus is the Son of God (v15) are the foundations that make love both possible and assured. By placing these doctrinal anchors in the middle of his love-teaching, John is saying: our ability to love comes from knowing and being known by God, not from our own emotional effort.
elements.mainPoint: Our love rests on **assurance of God dwelling in us**, shown by the Spirit, the apostles’ testimony and our confession of the Son.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: How does it pick up on some of the big themes in John and what does it have to do with love? Where does the assurance lie?

elements.passageText: 16And we have come to know and to believe the love that God has in us. God is love, and the one who resides in love resides in God, and God resides in him.

elements.question: Note that John repeats ‘God is love’ in v16b. What does it look like to ‘live in love’ and how does that give us confidence?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about what it means that “God is love” says who he is, not only what he does.
elements.questionHint: If “God is love“ is a statement about God’s very nature, what does that suggest about the permanence and reliability of the love that believers are called to live in?
elements.sampleAnswer: To “live in love“ means to inhabit a way of life shaped by the self-giving love God has shown us — loving other believers practically and sacrificially, just as God loved us in Christ. Because God himself is love, to live in love is to live in God, and God in us — it’s a mutual indwelling. This gives immense confidence because our security doesn’t rest on the quality of our feelings but on God’s own character and his commitment to dwell with those who trust him. The repetition of “God is love” reinforces that this love is utterly dependable: it is what God is, not merely something he does.
elements.mainPoint: Living in love means a **mutual dwelling with God**, whose settled character makes our security dependable.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: How does this pick up on earlier ideas?

elements.passageText: 17By this love is perfected with us, so that we may have confidence in the day of judgment, because just as Jesus is, so also are we in this world. 18There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear has to do with punishment. The one who fears punishment has not been perfected in love.

elements.question: How does v18 connect to what has gone before and how does it add to the confidence of v17?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask what John says fear is really about, and what back in verse 10 deals with it.
elements.questionHint:
What does John say fear is fundamentally “about” in v18?
How does that connect to what he said about the atoning sacrifice back in v10?
elements.sampleAnswer: Verse 17 has established that living in love gives us confidence for the day of judgment — we stand before God not in dread but with assurance, because our identity is bound up with Jesus. Verse 18 then explains the mechanism: perfect love expels fear, because fear is really about anticipated punishment. If we know that our sins have been atoned for (v10) and that we dwell in the God who is love, then the terror of judgment is displaced. The person who still lives in fear of punishment hasn’t yet fully grasped and rested in God’s love — but the more deeply we understand and receive that love, the more fear loses its grip on us.
elements.mainPoint: Fear of being punished is displaced when we know our **sins are atoned for** and we rest in God’s love.

elements.passageText:
19We love because he loved us first.

20If anyone says “I love God” and yet hates his fellow Christian, he is a liar, because the one who does not love his fellow Christian whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen. 21And the commandment we have from him is this: that the one who loves God should love his fellow Christian too.

elements.question: How do v19–21 tie up this whole section?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask how verse 19 sums up the whole section in a single sentence.
elements.questionHint:
How does v19 function as a summary of the whole passage?
What does it tell us about the relationship between God’s love and our love?
elements.sampleAnswer: These verses bring the entire section to a practical and logical conclusion. Verse 19 distils everything into a single sentence: our love for God and others is a response, not an initiative — “we love because he loved us first.” This encapsulates John’s whole argument that love flows from God’s prior action. Verses 20–21 then make the test explicit: you cannot genuinely claim to love an invisible God while hating a visible fellow-believer. Love for God and love for the Christian community are inseparable — one is the proof and expression of the other. The section that began with “let us love one another, because love is from God” ends with the same horizon: love God, and love your fellow Christian.
elements.mainPoint: Our love for God and people **answers his love first**; it cannot be genuine while we hate a fellow believer.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Looking at the whole section, what does perfect/complete love look like?

elements.text: 5:1–5: God’s children overcome the world as they trust in Jesus

elements.passageText:
1Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been fathered by God, and everyone who loves the father loves the child fathered by him. 2By this we know that we love the children of God: whenever we love God and obey his commandments. 3For this is the love of God: that we keep his commandments. And his commandments do not weigh us down, 4because everyone who has been fathered by God conquers the world. This is the conquering power that has conquered the world: our faith.

5Now who is the person who has conquered the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

elements.question: As John gets near the end of his letter, he draws the themes of faith, love and obedience together. What is the key point of faith in 5:1–5?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the two titles John uses for Jesus in verse 1 and verse 5.
elements.questionHint:
John mentions “the Christ” in v1 and “the Son of God” in v5.
Why do you think he is so specific about the content of the faith he’s describing?
elements.sampleAnswer: The key point of faith is belief in the specific identity of Jesus: that he is both “the Christ” (v1) and “the Son of God” (v5). This is not a vague or general belief in God, but a personal trust in Jesus as the one through whom God works salvation. This faith is what marks someone out as born of God (v1), what connects love for God with love for fellow believers (v1–2), and what is identified as the very power by which the world is overcome (v4–5). Faith in Jesus as the Son of God is therefore the integrating thread that holds love, obedience, and victory together.
elements.mainPoint: Genuine faith is **personal trust in Jesus’s identity as Messiah and divine Son**, the thread joining love, obedience and victory.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: How does John’s discussion of the work of the ‘Son of God’ in 4:7–21 help us understand what it means to believe that Jesus is the Son of God?

elements.passageText: 2By this we know that we love the children of God: whenever we love God and obey his commandments.

elements.question: Do you notice anything surprising about v2? How does this help us understand what John means?
elements.questionHintFirst: Compare which way the logic runs in verse 1 with the way it runs in verse 2.
elements.questionHint: Compare the direction of the logic in v1 with v2 — in which direction does each verse run, and why might John deliberately reverse the order?
elements.sampleAnswer: What’s surprising is that John reverses what we might expect. Earlier (v1) he said that loving God means loving God’s children — love for God leads to love for one another. But in v2 he says the way we know we love the children of God is when we love God and obey his commandments. So love for God proves love for others, and love for others proves love for God. The two can’t be separated and each one validates the other. This circularity is deliberate: John is showing that genuine Christian love is holistic and interlocking — you can’t isolate any one strand of it from the others.
elements.mainPoint: Love for God and love for believers **prove each other**, so neither can be separated from the other.

elements.passageText:
2By this we know that we love the children of God: whenever we love God and obey his commandments. 3For this is the love of God: that we keep his commandments. And his commandments do not weigh us down, 4because everyone who has been fathered by God conquers the world. This is the conquering power that has conquered the world: our faith.

5Now who is the person who has conquered the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

elements.question: Note that keeping the commands of God is part of loving the children of God. What do we learn about God’s commands here?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at verse 4 for the reason God’s commands are not a heavy load.
elements.questionHint: What reason does John give in v4 for why God’s commands don’t feel like a crushing burden — and what does that tell us about the relationship between obedience and faith?
elements.sampleAnswer: John makes two striking claims about God’s commands. First, they define what love for God actually looks like: keeping his commands is not a separate duty alongside love — it is love (v3). Second, and perhaps surprisingly, his commands are not burdensome (v3). The reason they don’t weigh us down is given immediately: because everyone born of God has already conquered the world (v4), and the conquering power is faith. In other words, obedience flows from a new nature and a secured victory — we don’t obey in order to earn God’s favour, but as the free response of those who are already his children and who have already won.
elements.mainPoint: Obeying God’s commands is **how love for him looks** and is not burdensome, because new birth and faith already give victory.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Observe the way John talks about the commands of God throughout his letter. How does that help us?

elements.passageText: 1Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been fathered by God, and everyone who loves the father loves the child fathered by him. 2By this we know that we love the children of God: whenever we love God and obey his commandments.

elements.question: What does it mean to be ‘born of God’ and what is the result of that?
elements.questionHintFirst: If a child shares a parent’s nature, what would you expect to see in someone fathered by God?
elements.questionHint: If a child shares the nature of their parent, what would you expect to be true of someone who has been “born of God” — and does John say anything about that here?
elements.sampleAnswer: To be “born of God” (or “fathered by God”) means to receive a new spiritual life from God himself — it describes genuine conversion and membership in God’s family. John says this is the result of believing that Jesus is the Christ (v1): faith and new birth are inseparably connected. The results of this new birth are also clear from these verses: you love God, you love the other children of God (v1–2), and you obey God’s commands (v2). Being born of God is therefore not merely a status but a transformative reality that reshapes how you love and how you live.
elements.mainPoint: Being born of God is **new spiritual life** that comes by believing, and it results in loving God and his people and obeying him.

16We have come to know love by this: that Jesus laid down his life for us; thus we ought to lay down our lives for our fellow Christians. 17But whoever has the world’s possessions and sees his fellow Christian in need and shuts off his compassion against him, how can the love of God reside in such a person?

18Little children, let us not love with word or with tongue but in deed and truth.

elements.question: What is love? What stops us from loving one another? What does it look like when we do?
When does it feel like the world is overcoming us? How do v1–5 reassure us? What does the ‘victorious’ Christian life look like?

elements.text:
John is bringing his letter to a close — and he does so with a remarkable series of confident, clear statements. ‘This is the testimony … this is the victory … this is the confidence … we know …’ After all the complexity of dealing with false teachers and the anxieties of his readers, John ends with certainty.

It is worth reflecting on how far we have come in this letter. John began with the eyewitness testimony of the apostles. He has addressed false claims about sin, about knowing God, about love. He has warned against antichrists. He has called his readers to love one another as God has loved them. Now he gathers it all together.

elements.question: As you read, look out for statements that start with ‘this is …’, and for any repeated words (e.g. ‘testimony/testify’, ‘water/blood’, Son, life, believes, etc.).

elements.text: 5:3–10: This is the victory: faith in the Son of God

elements.passageText:
3For this is the love of God: that we keep his commandments. And his commandments do not weigh us down, 4because everyone who has been fathered by God conquers the world. This is the conquering power that has conquered the world: our faith.

5Now who is the person who has conquered the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

elements.question: How does the world (and sometimes even Christians) think about ‘victory’ and ‘overcoming’? How are we to think about it as Christians?
elements.questionHintFirst: Find the single word John names as the conquering power in verse 4.
elements.questionHint: What single word does John use in v4 to name the “conquering power” — and does that match the way you normally think about what it means to overcome?
elements.sampleAnswer: The world typically measures victory in terms of power, success, social standing, or the defeat of opponents. Even Christians can fall into thinking that “overcoming” means experiencing freedom from all difficulty, achieving moral perfection, or winning in outward circumstances. But John defines the conquering power very specifically: it is faith (v4) — and in particular, faith that Jesus is the Son of God (v5). This isn’t a passive or passive-sounding thing; it is a confident, active trust in a person. Victory has already been accomplished through Jesus, and we participate in it by holding on to him in faith, not by our own achievement.
elements.mainPoint: Victory is **faith in Jesus as God’s Son**, already won and shared by trusting him, not worldly success or moral perfection.

elements.passageText: 6Jesus Christ is the one who came by water and blood—not by the water only, but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.

elements.question: How does John go on to define Jesus as the Son of God?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask what error “not by the water only” would be pushing back against.
elements.questionHint:
Why do you think John emphasises “not by the water only, but by the water and the blood”?
What view might he be pushing back against?
elements.sampleAnswer: John defines Jesus as the Son of God by the manner of his coming: he came “by water and blood.” He is emphatic that it is not the water only, but both the water and the blood. This appears to be a correction of a false teaching (likely associated with early Gnostic-type teachers) that separated the divine Christ from the human Jesus — suggesting perhaps that the divine element came at Jesus’s baptism but departed before the cross. John insists that the same Jesus who was baptised also shed his blood on the cross. The Spirit also testifies to this truth, and as “the truth” the Spirit’s witness is entirely reliable.
elements.mainPoint: Jesus came **by baptism and by the cross**, as one person, answering teaching that split the divine Christ from the man Jesus.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: What do you think he means by coming by ‘water and the blood’? What then does this mean about faith in Jesus?

elements.passageText:
7For there are three that testify, 8the Spirit and the water and the blood, and these three are in agreement.

9If we accept the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, because this is the testimony of God that he has testified concerning his Son.

elements.question: What reasons does John give for believing that Jesus is the Son of God? Why are these good reasons?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look at verse 9 for the argument from human testimony to God’s testimony.
elements.questionHint: What principle does John use in v9 to argue that God’s testimony is especially trustworthy — and where does that principle come from?
elements.sampleAnswer: John points to a threefold testimony: the Spirit, the water, and the blood — all three in agreement (v7–8). This matters because the Old Testament required two or three witnesses to establish truth (Deuteronomy 19:15), and here God supplies three. More importantly, v9 makes a simple but powerful argument: we routinely accept human testimony as sufficient grounds for belief — how much more should we accept the testimony of God himself, who has testified about his own Son? The authority of the witness is the strongest possible: it is God’s own word.
elements.mainPoint: Three agreeing witnesses, plus the principle that **God’s testimony outweighs human testimony**, give strong reasons to believe.

elements.passageText: 7For there are three that testify, 8the Spirit and the water and the blood, and these three are in agreement.

elements.question: Why is it important that ‘the Spirit and the water and the blood’ are in agreement?
elements.questionHintFirst: Imagine the three witnesses disagreeing and ask what that would do to our confidence.
elements.questionHint: If the three witnesses disagreed with one another, what problems would that create for our confidence in who Jesus is?
elements.sampleAnswer: The agreement of all three is important because it means there is no internal contradiction in the testimony about Jesus. The false teachers in John’s context may have tried to drive a wedge between different aspects of Jesus’s identity — separating the spiritual from the physical, or the baptism from the crucifixion. But if the Spirit, the water (baptism), and the blood (cross) all testify to the same thing, then the whole of Jesus’s ministry and the whole of God’s revelation points consistently to the one truth: Jesus is the Son of God who came in the flesh to save. A unanimous witness is much harder to dismiss.
elements.mainPoint: Because the Spirit, baptism and the cross agree, the testimony is **consistent and hard to dismiss** against teachers who divided Jesus’s identity.

elements.text: 5:11–13: This is the testimony: eternal life in the Son of God

elements.passageText: 11And this is the testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.

elements.question: We have been urged by John to accept the testimony of God about his Son, but what is that testimony?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice where John says eternal life is found.
elements.questionHint:
Notice that John says eternal life is “in” the Son.
What does that suggest about how we receive this life?
elements.sampleAnswer: The testimony is a gift and a location: “God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.” So the content of God’s testimony is not merely doctrinal information but a declaration of what God has done. He has freely given eternal life, and that life is not an abstract blessing — it is bound up with a person, the Son. To have the Son is to have this life; to lack the Son is to lack it entirely (v12). The testimony is both good news and an urgent summons: eternal life is available, and it is found in Jesus.
keyTerms: in the son|in his son|in jesus|person|located|found in
elements.mainPoint: The testimony is **a gift bound to a person**: life that never ends has been given to us, and it is located in the Son.

elements.passageText:
10(The one who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself; the one who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has testified concerning his Son.) 11And this is the testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. 12The one who has the Son has this eternal life; the one who does not have the Son of God does not have this eternal life.

13I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life.

elements.question: What does it mean to ‘have the Son’? How does it fit with what we have already seen in this passage?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about how “the testimony in himself” links inner faith to the outward marks John has described.
elements.questionHint:
John says the believer has “the testimony in himself” (v10).
How do you think receiving the Son inwardly connects to the outward marks of faith John has described throughout the letter?
elements.sampleAnswer: To “have the Son” means to believe in him (v10, 13) — to trust personally in Jesus as the Son of God. It is not just intellectual assent; it involves receiving him so that, as v10 says, the believer has the testimony in himself. This fits with everything John has already said: faith in Jesus as the Christ and Son of God leads to new birth (5:1), to love for God and others (5:2), to the indwelling Spirit (4:13), and to life (5:12). “Having the Son” is therefore the heart of the whole Christian life — all the other marks of genuine faith flow from this personal trust in Jesus.
elements.mainPoint: To have the Son is **to trust him personally**, and every other mark of genuine faith flows from that.

elements.passageText: 13I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life.

elements.question: Where else in 1 John has he talked about ‘eternal life’? How do those earlier references fit with what he says here?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look back at 1:2 and 2:25 and notice what eternal life is in each.
elements.questionHint:
Think back to the very opening of the letter.
What did John say “eternal life” actually was?
How does that shape what it means to “have” it here?
elements.sampleAnswer: John mentions eternal life right at the start of his letter (1:2), where he describes the “eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us” — identifying eternal life with the person of Jesus himself. He also mentions it in 2:25, where he says that eternal life is what God has promised to those who remain in the Son and the Father. This fits perfectly with 5:11–13: eternal life is not a new concept John introduces at the end, but the thread running through the whole letter. To have Jesus is to have life. The letter ends, as it began, with this life-giving reality at the centre.
elements.mainPoint: Eternal life runs through the letter from its opening, where it is Jesus himself, to the promise to those who remain in him, so **the end matches the beginning**.

elements.question: How might this reassure John’s readers (v13)?
elements.questionHintFirst: Compare “know”, “think” and “hope”, and decide which word John chose and why it matters.
elements.questionHint: What word does John use — “know,” “think,” or “hope” — and why does that choice of word matter so much for John’s anxious readers?
elements.sampleAnswer: John explicitly states his pastoral purpose here: he has written “so that you may know that you have eternal life.” His readers had been unsettled by false teachers who may have questioned whether they truly belonged to God. But John cuts through that uncertainty: if you believe in the name of the Son of God, then you can know — not merely hope or guess — that you have eternal life right now. The assurance is direct, personal, and present-tense. The letter itself becomes a means of building and sustaining the confidence of genuine believers.
keyTerms: not hope|not merely|not guess|rather than hope|hope|guess
elements.mainPoint: John wants believers to **know, not merely hope**, that they have eternal life now.

elements.text: 5:14–17: This is the confidence: approaching God in prayer

elements.passageText: 14And this is the confidence that we have before him: that whenever we ask anything according to his will, he hears us.

elements.question: What confidence does the believer have from knowing that eternal life is in Jesus?
elements.questionHintFirst: Notice the condition John attaches to asking in verse 14.
elements.questionHint:
What qualification does John include in v14?
What does that qualification tell us about the kind of relationship prayer is meant to reflect?
elements.sampleAnswer: The confidence flows directly from the relationship established by eternal life in Jesus. Because believers are God’s children — born of God, indwelt by his Spirit, secure in his love — they have the freedom to approach him in prayer. Specifically, John says that when we ask according to God’s will, he hears us (v14), and if he hears us, we can be confident that we already have what we’ve asked (v15). This isn’t a vending-machine approach to prayer but a child-like trust: knowing that our Father is attentive to us and that his will is good. Assurance of eternal life gives prayer its foundation.
elements.mainPoint: Secure as God’s children, believers approach him freely, **trusting that he listens when they pray in line with what he wants**.

elements.passageText: 16If anyone sees his fellow Christian committing a sin not resulting in death, he should ask, and God will grant life to the person who commits a sin not resulting in death. There is a sin resulting in death. I do not say that he should ask about that. 17All unrighteousness is sin, but there is sin not resulting in death.

elements.question: What qualification does John give and what example of prayer does he give?
elements.questionHintFirst: Ask why John’s example is praying for someone else rather than for yourself.
elements.questionHint: What does it reveal about John’s understanding of prayer that his main example is praying for someone else who is sinning, rather than praying for yourself?
elements.sampleAnswer: John qualifies his teaching on confident prayer by introducing the category of “sin resulting in death” alongside “sin not resulting in death” (v16–17). The example of prayer he gives is intercessory: if you see a fellow Christian sinning in a way that does not lead to death, you should pray for them, and God will grant them life. This is a beautiful example of praying according to God’s will — his will being that his people live and are restored. For the sin that does lead to death, John declines to instruct his readers to pray, though he doesn’t forbid it; this is likely a reference to the kind of wholesale rejection of Christ represented by the false teachers who have “gone out.”
keyTerms: death|not lead|leads to death|lead to death
elements.mainPoint: John’s example is **intercession for a sinning fellow believer**, asking for restoration, and he separates sin that does and does not lead to death.

elements.question: How does what John has already said about sin in the letter help us understand what he means by ‘a sin not resulting in death’ and ‘a sin resulting in death’?
elements.questionHintFirst: Remember what John has already said about those who deny that Jesus is the Christ.
elements.questionHint: What has John already said earlier in his letter about people who deny that Jesus is the Christ — and could that help clarify what he means by “sin resulting in death”?
elements.sampleAnswer: Throughout the letter John has insisted that Christians do sin (1:8–10), but that the genuine child of God does not persist in wilful, habitual sin as a pattern of life (3:6–9). He has also shown that the false teachers — the antichrists — represent a terminal departure from the truth about Jesus: they have denied that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh (2:22–23; 4:2–3) and have “gone out from us” (2:19). In that light, “sin not resulting in death” is likely the ongoing but confessed and repented sin of a genuine believer — which can be met with prayer and restoration. “Sin resulting in death” likely refers to the deliberate, final rejection of Christ that the false teachers embody — a hardened rejection of Christ by people who were never truly his, rather than ordinary moral failure.
elements.mainPoint: A sin resulting in death is probably **the final rejection of Christ** shown by the false teachers, while ordinary confessed sin can be prayed over and restored.

elements.text: 5:18–21: Safety in the Son

elements.passageText: 18We know that everyone fathered by God does not sin, but God protects the one he has fathered, and the evil one cannot touch him. 19We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one. 20And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us insight to know him who is true, and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This one is the true God and eternal life. 21Little children, guard yourselves from idols.

elements.question: How do the closing verses of the letter pick up on the themes we have seen throughout?
elements.questionHintFirst: Look for a word or phrase in each closing verse that you have met earlier in the letter.
elements.questionHint: Can you find a word or phrase in each of these final verses that echoes something John said earlier in the letter?
elements.sampleAnswer: These verses draw together almost every major thread of the letter. The “we know” structure mirrors John’s repeated concern to give his readers certain knowledge rather than doubt. The statement that God’s children do not sin (v18) echoes 3:6–9. The protection of the believer by God himself (v18) recalls 4:4 (“the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world”). The world lying under the power of the evil one (v19) connects to John’s repeated warnings about the world and its false spirit. The Son of God coming to give us insight (v20) echoes the prologue’s concern with what has been seen and testified. And the identification of Jesus as “the true God and eternal life” brings the whole letter full circle to its opening declaration about the Word of life.
elements.mainPoint: The closing verses **echo the whole letter**: assurance, the evil one, the world, the Son, true knowledge and eternal life.

elements.question: How do these closing verses pick up on John’s aim of reassuring his readers?
elements.questionHintFirst: Count how often John says “we know” here and notice what each one covers.
elements.questionHint:
John uses “we know” three times in these verses.
What is the effect of that repeated phrase on a reader who has been feeling uncertain about their faith?
elements.sampleAnswer: John’s pastoral aim throughout the letter has been to give his readers confidence in the face of false teachers who have unsettled them. These verses offer reassurance on three fronts, each introduced by “we know.” First, God himself protects those he has fathered — the evil one cannot ultimately touch them (v18). Second, despite the world being under the power of the evil one, believers are “from God” (v19) — their identity and security are not in the world but in God. Third, the Son of God has come and given them real, reliable insight to know the true God — and they are already “in him” (v20). Each “we know” is a further nail of certainty driven into the anxiety the false teachers have tried to exploit.
elements.mainPoint: Three certainties, God’s protection, belonging to him rather than the world, and the Son’s gift of understanding, **steady anxious readers**.

elements.question: Why do you think John ends the letter as he does?
elements.questionHintFirst: Think about what could be offered in place of Jesus, and why John ends so abruptly.
elements.questionHint: Given that John has spent the whole letter insisting that Jesus is the true God and the source of eternal life, what might the warning to “guard yourselves from idols” be pointing to?
elements.sampleAnswer: John ends with a bold declaration — “This one is the true God and eternal life” — and then an abrupt warning: “guard yourselves from idols.” The contrast is striking and deliberate. Having spent the whole letter pointing his readers to what is true, real, and living — Jesus Christ — he closes with a warning not to substitute anything else in his place. In a world full of competing religious claims, the danger for John’s readers (and for us) is always that something or someone else will occupy the place that belongs to Jesus alone. The brevity and sharpness of v21 gives the letter real urgency: in the light of everything John has said, don’t settle for anything less than the true God.
elements.mainPoint: Having shown that Jesus is truly God and life, John urgently warns against **letting any substitute take his place**.
