blocks.title: People who struggle with assurance
blocks.body: If you find yourself wondering whether you are really a Christian — whether your faith is genuine, whether God truly accepts you, whether you really belong to him — this letter was written for you. 1 John is not a test designed to produce anxiety. John states his purpose plainly at the end: ‘I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life.’ (5:13, NET). The goal is confidence, not doubt.

blocks.title: People unsettled by false teaching
blocks.body: John wrote into a specific crisis: people had left the community, and their departure had shaken those who remained. If you have ever been confused by confident-sounding teaching that seemed to undermine what you believed, or by Christians who seemed more certain and more impressive but whose message felt subtly different, this letter speaks directly to that experience.

blocks.title: People who want to go deeper in 1 John
blocks.body: The letter is only five chapters long, but it is theologically rich and structurally complex. This study moves through it carefully, paying attention to what John actually says in context rather than lifting out familiar verses in isolation. Whether you are new to 1 John or have read it many times, working through it closely is likely to surface things you have not noticed before.

blocks.title: On your own
blocks.body: This study works well as a personal study. Each session begins with a prompt to read the relevant passage — take that seriously, since the questions are designed to reward close attention to John’s actual words. Write your answers as you go, and give the reflection questions at the end real time. 1 John rewards slow, attentive reading more than speed.

blocks.title: In a group
blocks.body: The study works well in a small group setting. The most rewarding approach is usually for each person to work through the session individually first, writing their answers, and then for the group to come together to compare what they found. The themes of light, love, and assurance generate rich discussion — and because John’s letter was written to a community, reading it together has a particular fittingness.

blocks.title: Read the whole letter first
blocks.body: 1 John is short enough to read in one sitting — about twenty minutes. The first chapter of this study includes the full text, and you are encouraged to read or listen to all five chapters before beginning. Seeing the whole letter at once makes each individual session significantly richer, and helps you see how John’s recurring themes build and interweave.

blocks.title: Working with a leader or mentor
blocks.body:
If someone has recommended this study to you — a pastor, a small group leader, or a trusted friend — that relationship matters. 1 John raises personal questions about assurance, love, and what genuine faith looks like in practice. Having someone to think those questions through with can make the difference between the letter producing its intended comfort and it becoming a source of unnecessary anxiety.

At the end of each chapter, the Share button lets you send your written answers directly to your leader or mentor — via WhatsApp, email, or any other app on your phone. This gives them a window into your thinking before you meet, and makes for a much richer conversation.

blocks.title: Leaders’ Notes
blocks.body: Leaders’ Notes are included with this study but are switched off by default. To read them, open Settings → App → Optional Pages and switch on Leaders’ Notes (this needs Intermediate interface mode). They are aimed at group leaders and mentors.

blocks.title: Two kinds of questions
blocks.body: Each session has two kinds of questions. The Bible questions follow the passage closely — asking you to look carefully at what John actually says, in context. The reflection questions at the end turn the same material toward you personally, asking what John’s message means for your own faith and life. Both kinds matter: the Bible questions build the foundation; the reflection questions are where the letter does its pastoral work.

blocks.title: Keeping John’s purpose in view
blocks.body: Some verses in 1 John can feel challenging or even alarming when read in isolation — especially those about sin, love, and what it means to ‘remain’ in God. As you work through the questions, keep John’s stated purpose in mind: he is writing to give assurance to believers, not to undermine it. When a verse feels difficult, the first question to ask is: how does this fit with what John is trying to achieve?

blocks.title: The ‘tests’ in 1 John
blocks.body: You may have encountered approaches to 1 John that present it as a series of ‘tests’ — of belief, love, and obedience — to apply to yourself. This study takes a wider view. Those same markers did two jobs for John’s first readers: they exposed the claims of the false teachers who had unsettled them, and they reassured the people who were trusting Christ. They can still help us examine ourselves honestly, but always so that we look to Christ and are assured by him, not as a checklist for earning assurance. Keeping both jobs in view makes a significant difference to how the letter reads.

intro: These notes are designed to help group leaders get the most out of each study — both for the people they are leading and for themselves. They are not a substitute for working through the material yourself first.
Remember the purpose of 1 John. The letter is written to reassure believers (1 John 5:13), not to produce anxious self-examination. Keep coming back to that pastoral aim as you lead.

Don’t turn the ‘tests’ inward too quickly. The tests John gives (belief, love, sin) first exposed the false teachers and reassured John’s readers. Self-examination has its place, but not as a checklist, and not to the point of despair.

Watch for the person spiralling into doubt. 1 John contains some of the most comforting and some of the most challenging verses in the New Testament. Your job is to hold both together and point people to the reassurance John intends.

keyPoints.body:
The structure of 1 John is complex but not unstructured. Different scholars see two halves, a chiasm, and other patterns — and more than one may be present simultaneously. It is probably safest to acknowledge the complexity rather than impose a single grid.

A key structural marker: 1:1–2:13 is dominated by present tense verbs, while 2:14–5:21 is dominated by aorist verbs. This is very clear in the Greek. The first section also uses light/darkness imagery; the second section is full of ‘world’ language. The passage 2:12–14 appears to function as a pivot between the two halves.

The letter reads at points like a sermon on Jesus’ farewell discourse in John’s Gospel — there are extensive echoes throughout. Helping your group see those connections will enrich their reading.

The purpose statement in 5:13 (‘so that you may know that you have eternal life’) is the interpretive key to the whole letter. Everything John writes is in service of that goal: reassurance, not anxiety.

pastorals.body:
The so-called ‘three tests’ approach (belief, love, obedience to commands) is widely used but can be pastorally unhelpful if applied only as a personal checklist, because applying them introspectively can lead to despair rather than assurance — the opposite of John’s aim.

A more helpful framing: the tests are best used first externally, to evaluate the claims of false teachers who were unsettling the believers, and then, gently, to reassure those who trust Christ. That reorientation will help your group engage the letter more fruitfully throughout the series.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for people who come into this series already anxious about their standing before God. The letter is meant to be medicine, not a further burden. Establish early on that John’s goal is to give assurance, not undermine it.

keyPoints.body:
We don’t know precisely what the ‘antichrists’ were teaching, but their effect was to destabilise the believers’ confidence. They likely claimed some form of spiritual superiority. John writes to counteract that.

The concept of ‘Antichrist’ was not John’s invention — it was a familiar idea in Jewish apocalyptic literature of the period. John applies it to the false teachers who had left the community (v.19).

The ‘tests’ function diagnostically here: when you encounter someone claiming spiritual authority, ask — what do they say about Jesus? How do they treat fellow believers? How do they relate to sin? These questions expose the false teacher, not the anxious believer.

Structurally, note the tense shift: everything up to 2:13 is present-tense dominated (light/darkness imagery); from 2:14 onwards the aorist tense dominates (world language). This passage sits at the hinge of the letter.

pastorals.body:
The most effective false teachers are often plausible, spiritual, and experienced. Help your group think carefully about subtle distortions, not just outright denial. Does this teacher’s message centre on Jesus and his cross? Or does it offer something extra — a programme, a method, a higher spirituality — alongside or instead of the cross?

The reassurance of this passage is direct: your sins have been forgiven, you know the Father, you have the anointing. Don’t let the warning about antichrists overshadow the warmth of what John says to the believers themselves.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for subtle false teaching that doesn’t deny the cross outright but quietly displaces it — teaching that adds requirements for spiritual maturity, focuses on leaders or methods rather than Christ, or suggests that other believers are spiritually compromised.

keyPoints.body:
This section is likely the third in a sequence beginning at 2:15: first, don’t love the world; second, loving the world is tempting because of the antichrists; third, it is hard because God’s children aren’t yet what they will be. The tension between present identity and future glory is central.

The most challenging verses are 3:4–6 and 3:9, which seem to say that those who are born of God do not sin — apparently contradicting chapter 1. These must be read in light of the whole letter, not in isolation.

Two approaches help: (1) the ‘habitual sin’ reading (John Stott) — the true believer does not make a practice of sin; (2) the ‘specific sin’ reading — John uses ‘sin’ elsewhere (John 15:22; 16:8; 6:28; 1 John 5:16–17) to refer specifically to the sin of rejecting Jesus. On this reading, 3:9 refers to the particular sin of departing from apostolic teaching and denying Christ, not to sin in general.

pastorals.body:
Neither solution to 3:9 is perfect, but both are better than taking the verse in isolation. The most important pastoral move is to read these verses in the context of the whole book — especially chapter 1 — and to keep John’s stated purpose (reassurance) at the centre.

Be alert to anyone who uses these verses to move toward a sinless perfectionism. Equally, be alert to anyone so troubled by the apparent standard that they conclude they cannot be a Christian at all. Both need to be gently redirected to the full picture John paints.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for the temptation to land too firmly on one interpretation of 3:9 and present it as settled. Acknowledging the genuine difficulty here, while keeping the pastoral goal clear, is more honest and more helpful.

keyPoints.body:
The call to love one another is grounded not in feelings but in the concrete example of Christ (3:16). Love is defined by action, not emotion.

On confidence before God (3:19–22): note that the basis for assurance here is not how well we are loving, but simply whether we are showing love for the people of God. The bar is directional, not perfectionist.

The test for spirits in 4:1–6 returns to the letter’s core diagnostic: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. The Christological question remains the primary one.

pastorals.body:
For those with a sensitive conscience, 3:20 (‘God is greater than our conscience’) is an important pastoral word: God’s knowledge of us is more reliable than our own self-assessment. This cuts against both complacency and excessive self-doubt.

On spotting false teaching: again, the distortion is often subtle. Does this teaching require something extra? Does it focus on a person, leader, or method rather than the cross? Are the teachers characterised by doing what is right and loving the brothers?

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for those who use the command to love as a source of anxiety (‘Am I loving enough?’) rather than as a description of the direction of their life. Gently reframe: the question is not perfection, but orientation.

keyPoints.body:
This passage contains some of 1 John’s most quoted verses, which means they are also among its most frequently read out of context. Keep returning to the situation John is addressing and his overall aim of reassurance.

Love in this passage is defined by what God has done, not by emotional experience. ‘God is love’ (4:8, 16) is a statement about God’s character as revealed in the sending of his Son — not a general claim that love equals God, or that anyone who loves is therefore in God.

Most of the ‘command’ language in 1 John appears in a love context, suggesting it is being used in the same technical sense as Jesus’ ‘new command’ in John 13:34. The repetition of ‘God sent his Son’ grounds the whole section.

pastorals.body:
Be careful not to allow 4:16 to become a proof text for the idea that God is in whoever loves in a general sense, regardless of whether they confess Jesus. John is writing to believers about their love for one another within the community of faith, not making a universal claim about all human love.

The connection between love and the absence of fear (4:18) is deeply pastoral. Many in your group may be operating with a fear-based faith. This passage invites them into something more like the security of a child who knows they are loved.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for the person who finds ‘God is love’ easy to affirm but struggles to feel it. The passage is full of objective grounds for confidence — don’t rush past them to application before the group has actually sat with what God has done.

keyPoints.body:
The final section gathers up the whole letter in a run of confident statements: this is the victory, this is the testimony, this is the confidence, and “we know”. Help your group to notice how many earlier themes return here: faith in the Son, the Spirit’s testimony, eternal life, obedience and love, the evil one and the world.

The “water and the blood” (5:6) is difficult, and your group does not need to settle every detail. The most likely point is that Jesus’ identity is bound up with both his baptism and his death, against teaching that separated the heavenly Christ from the man Jesus. What matters for the group is that John offers testimony that agrees, resting finally on what God himself has said about his Son.

Verse 13 is the purpose statement that ties the letter together. Eternal life is something believers already have in the Son (vv. 11–12), not a status to be earned. The closing verses (vv. 18–21) are deliberately abrupt: three times “we know”, then a warning about idols. Having called the Son “the true God and eternal life”, John warns against letting anything else take his place.

pastorals.body:
Verses 16–17 (a “sin resulting in death”) are among the hardest in the letter, and the cause of more anxiety than almost any other. Christians have understood them in more than one way. The study suggests one likely reading, a final and settled rejection of Christ of the kind shown by those who left, without treating it as the only possibility. Do not let the group spend the whole session trying to define it.

Be gentle with anyone who fears that they have committed this sin. Nothing in the passage suggests that worry about one’s own standing is itself a sign of it, and John’s stated aim in 5:13 is to give assurance. If someone is deeply distressed, encourage them to talk it through privately with a pastor or trusted mentor.

On prayer (5:14–15): some in your group will be carrying prayers that have not been answered. “According to his will” is not a loophole, nor a test of how much faith they have. It describes the security of a child who knows they are heard. Avoid any suggestion that unanswered prayer means they lacked faith.

watch.body: 👁️ Watch for the group getting stuck on 5:6–8 or 5:16–17 and running out of time before the confident statements of 5:13–15 and 5:18–21. Come back deliberately to 5:13. As this is the last session, leave a few minutes to look back over the whole letter: what has John helped each person to know?

body: These notes go alongside the six sessions. Do each session first and write your own answers, then read the matching chapter here. They do not repeat the questions. They give background, explain difficult words and verses, and say plainly where Christians read a passage in different ways.

John’s first letter is not an essay with a tidy outline. He comes back again and again to three things, believing the truth about Jesus, obeying God and loving one another, and looks at each from a new angle. His purpose, stated near the end, is that his readers may know that they have eternal life (5:13). Keep that in mind as you read.

The letter was written to Christians who had been shaken. Some people had left their fellowship (2:19), and the teaching of those who left was unsettling those who stayed. You will see that background in many of these notes.
Where the Bible is quoted, the translation is the NET. The small raised numbers are footnotes: tap one to read it.

footnotes.body: ‘The word of life’ can mean the message about life, or the one who is Life himself. Most Christian readers hear both: the message cannot be separated from the person.
John’s verb for ‘cleanses’ in verse 7 is in the present tense, which suggests a cleansing that goes on and not a single event in the past.

The Greek word is translated in various ways: ‘propitiation’, ‘atoning sacrifice’, ‘expiation’. The first stresses that Jesus’ death turns aside God’s righteous anger against sin; the second stresses that it removes guilt. Many Christians, in the Reformed tradition and beyond, hold that both ideas are present. John uses the same word in 4:10.

In 3:15–17 John shows that withholding help from someone in need is a way of failing to love; ‘hate’ can cover that. Where the NET says ‘fellow Christian’ in these verses, John’s Greek word is ‘brother’; it means a fellow believer and includes women as well as men.

setting.header: Why John begins as he does
setting.body:
The letter opens with no greeting and no name. John goes straight to what matters: the apostles have heard, seen and touched the one who is life itself. He begins like this because his readers have been told that the apostles’ message is not enough. John answers by pointing back to what was there from the beginning, the same word that opens his Gospel.[[fn:1]] The message is not one opinion among many. It comes from people who knew Jesus.

‘Fellowship’ in verse 3 is not simply friendship. It means sharing something together, here the life that the apostles have with the Father and the Son. The readers are invited into the relationship the apostles already enjoy, and that is a reason for joy (v. 4).

claims.body:
Between 1:6 and 1:10 John says ‘if we say’ three times. Each is a claim that some in his day were making, and each gets a reply.

The claimWhat it overlooksJohn’s reply
We have fellowship with God (1:6)God is light, so we cannot share his life while living in the darkWalk in the light; Jesus’ blood keeps on cleansing (v. 7)
We have no sin (1:8)The sin that is still in usConfess, and God forgives and cleanses (v. 9)
We have not sinned (1:10)God’s own verdict on usSuch a claim makes God a liar (v. 10)
But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous, forgiving us our sins and cleansing us from all unrighteousness. (1 John 1:9, NET)

Notice the pattern. John does not say that Christians never sin. He says that honest confession belongs to the life of a believer, and that God deals with sin on the basis of what Jesus has done.[[fn:2]]

light.body:
‘Walking in the light’ does not mean being sinless. John’s next words (2:1) show that he expects his readers still to sin. It means living openly before God, with no pretence, no hiding and no trying to look better than we are. In the light we see ourselves as we are, and we see Jesus as the one who deals with it.

That is why verse 7 links walking in the light with fellowship with other believers. A church that walks in the light is a place where people can admit failure and be forgiven.

advocate.header: Key idea: our advocate and the atoning sacrifice
advocate.body: John writes so that his readers will not sin. But he adds that if anyone does, Jesus, who is righteous, speaks for them with the Father (2:1–2). He can do so because he is himself the sacrifice that deals with sin.[[fn:3]] John says that this sacrifice is for the whole world. Christians understand that phrase in different ways: some take it to mean that the sacrifice is sufficient for everyone, others that John is thinking of people from every nation and not only of Jews. Whichever view you hold, the point John presses is that for anyone who comes to Jesus, no sin is beyond the sacrifice.

command.header: An old command that is also new (2:7–11)
command.body:
John calls the command he is writing about both old and new. It is old because his readers have had it from the very beginning of their Christian lives; it is not a fresh teaching. It is new because, in Christ, it is now truly being lived out as the darkness fades and the light shines.

The command is to love one another, as the next verses show. John is blunt: someone who says he is in the light but hates a fellow believer is still in the dark. ‘Hate’ in John’s writing does not always mean active hostility. It can include a cold indifference that refuses to love.[[fn:4]] The test is practical, and it is open to everyone.

footnotes.body: John also changes from ‘I am writing’ to ‘I wrote’. Commentators explain this in several ways, and little depends on it.
In John 3:16 God loves the world: that is, people in rebellion. The love forbidden here is love for the world’s way of life, not love for the people in it.
Some commentators think the ‘anointing’ means the gospel message itself. The two ideas are close, since the Spirit works with the message.

groups.body: In 2:12–14 John addresses three groups twice. Readers have understood this in different ways. Some think he means three age ranges in the congregation. Others think all his readers are ‘children’, and that he singles out two kinds of maturity: those who have known God for a long time and those who have been strong in the fight.[[fn:1]] Either way the point is the same. John is not scolding. He reminds them of what is already true of them, their sins forgiven, God known and the evil one overcome, before he warns them about the world and about false teaching.

world.body:
‘The world’ has several meanings in John’s writings. It can mean the created order, the people God made, or human society organised against God. In 2:15–17 it is the last of these. That is how John can tell us not to love the world while his Gospel says that God loved it.[[fn:2]]

The three things he lists are cravings that come from our fallen nature, longing for what we see, and pride in what we have. They are habits of the heart more than objects to avoid. They are not from the Father, John says, and they are passing away; the person who does God’s will remains for ever (v. 17).

lastHour.header: The last hour and the antichrists
lastHour.body:
The New Testament treats the ‘last days’ as beginning with Jesus’ first coming, and John’s ‘last hour’ belongs to that. Its mark, he says, is that many antichrists have come. They are not a distant figure. They were once inside the church (2:19), and they deny that Jesus is the Christ (2:22).

Christians have held different views about whether one final antichrist will appear before the end. John knows that his readers have heard about such a figure (2:18), and he says that the spirit of antichrist is already at work. The practical point is stronger than the debate: the test of any teaching is what it says about Jesus.

anointing.body:
John tells his readers that they have an anointing from the Holy One and that they know the truth (2:20, 27). Most Christians understand the anointing as the Holy Spirit, given to every believer, who confirms the apostles’ teaching in their hearts.[[fn:3]]

This does not mean that no one needs a teacher; John is teaching in this very letter. It means that they do not need to go looking for new teachers with a secret message, because what they heard at the start is what the Spirit confirms.

As for you, what you have heard from the beginning must remain in you. If what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father. (1 John 2:24, NET)

sonFather.header: Key idea: the Father and the Son go together
sonFather.body: A thought that keeps returning in these verses is that no one can have the Father while rejecting the Son (2:22–23). Whatever else a teaching says about God, John asks first what it does with Jesus.

footnotes.body: In Greek the present tense can describe a repeated or continuing action, but it does not always. That is why the argument rests on the whole context, and not on the tense alone.
‘Seed’ in 3:9 is explained in different ways: the Holy Spirit, the new life God gives, or the word of God. Each fits the idea of something from God that stays in the believer.

hope.body:
Verse 28 looks ahead to Christ’s return. John wants his readers to meet him with confidence and not with shame, and the way there is to remain in him now. The next verses give the reason. We are already God’s children, though what we shall be has not yet been shown; we know that when he appears we shall be like him.

Dear friends, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that whenever it is revealed we will be like him, because we will see him just as he is. (1 John 3:2, NET)

That hope, John adds, changes how we live now (3:3). The hope does not earn anything. The change follows from it.

practice.body:
Verses 4–10 are among the hardest in the letter. John says that no one born of God practises sin, and that such a person cannot go on sinning (3:6, 9). Yet in 1:8–2:2 he has said that anyone who claims to be without sin is deceiving himself, and that Christians who sin have an advocate. How can both be true?

Several answers have been given. One is that John describes an ongoing way of life: not that believers never commit a sin, but that sin is no longer the pattern they live by.[[fn:1]] Another is that he describes the new nature God gives, which will one day be fully seen. Some have thought that he means only deliberate sin, but John gives no sign of limiting the word in that way.

This study leans towards the first two answers together. John is describing people whose basic direction has been changed by new birth. The wording about birth, about God’s ‘seed’ and about the family supports this.[[fn:2]] Whatever solution you prefer, John plainly expects his readers still to sin (2:1), so he cannot be teaching that Christians reach a stage when they no longer sin.

families.body:
God’s childrenThe devil’s children
Where they come fromBorn of God (3:9)Follow the devil, who has sinned from the beginning (3:8)
What marks themPractise righteousness and love fellow believers (3:10)Practise sin and fail to love (3:8, 10)
What Jesus came to doTake away sins (3:5)Destroy the devil’s works (3:8)

John draws the line sharply on purpose. Some in his day were saying that what a person does has little to do with whether they know God.

troubled.header: If you are troubled by your own sin
troubled.body: John gives no comfort to anyone who treats sin lightly. But sorrow over sin, the wish to be free of it and the readiness to confess (1:9) belong with new birth, and a Christian who is troubled in this way is not usually the person John describes. To the believer who is struggling, he points to the advocate (2:1).

footnotes.body: Where the NET says ‘fellow Christian’ or ‘brothers and sisters’ here and in 2:9–11, John’s Greek word is ‘brother’; it means a fellow believer and includes women.
Some translations say ‘heart’ where the NET says ‘conscience’. The Greek word is ‘heart’, understood here as the inner voice that judges us.

‘Come in the flesh’ means that the Son of God truly became human. Some in John’s day seem to have taught that the divine Christ only appeared to be human, or left Jesus before the cross; John’s words here, and in 5:6, answer that.

cain.body:
John uses Cain as the pattern of hatred. Cain killed his brother[[fn:1]] because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s were righteous (3:12). Hatred, John says, is murder in the heart (3:15), and it follows that the world’s hostility to believers should be no surprise: righteousness shows up what is wrong.

Verse 14 is easy to misread. John does not say that we pass from death to life by loving. He says that we know we have passed from death to life because we love. Love is the evidence of a life already given, not the way to get it.

costs.body:
John’s pattern for love is Christ, who gave his life for us. He then brings it to ordinary things. If someone has enough, sees a fellow believer in need and closes his heart, how can God’s love be in him? John tells us to love in action and in truth, not only in words.

Little children, let us not love with word or with tongue but in deed and truth. (1 John 3:18, NET)

That is a high standard, but a concrete one. It begins with money, time and attention.

conscience.body:
These two verses are famous for being hard to translate.[[fn:2]] The usual reading is that they bring comfort. When our conscience condemns us, perhaps because we know how often we fail to love as we should, God is greater than that voice. He knows everything, including a love that we cannot always see in ourselves.

A few readers hear a warning instead: if our conscience condemns us, God, who knows more, will condemn us more. But the context is about reassurance, so this study follows the comfort reading. Notice that John assumes we look honestly at ourselves; he does not tell us to stop. He tells us what to do with what we find: bring it to God, who is greater.

spirits.body:
John’s warning not to believe every spirit refers to every voice that claims to speak for God. The test is not how impressive the speaker is or how powerful the experience was, but what the voice says about Jesus: does it confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (4:2)?[[fn:3]] The same test appears in 2:22. A teaching that makes Jesus less than the true, human Son of God has the spirit of antichrist.

John adds a second test: who listens to the apostles’ message (4:6). He also gives his readers an assurance: the one who is in them is greater than the one who is in the world (4:4). The tests are given to protect the weak, not to make Christians suspicious of everyone.

footnotes.body: Commentators differ about exactly what ‘his love is perfected in us’ means: whether it is God’s love for us, our love for him, or both together, and what it is for love to be ‘perfected’.

source.body:
John says that God is love (4:8, 16). He does not say that love is God. The point is that God’s character is the source of everything that deserves the name of love, and that we learn what love is from what God has done and not from our feelings. He has defined it for us at the cross.

In this is love: not that we have loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins. (1 John 4:10, NET)

So love is not first of all our achievement. The command to love one another rests on a love that came to us before we loved anyone, and we love in response to it (4:19).

unseen.header: No one has ever seen God (4:12)
unseen.body: John returns to a thought from his Gospel: God cannot be seen directly, and the Son has made him known. Here he adds that if we love one another, God remains in us and his love reaches its goal in us. ‘His love’ can be taken as God’s love for us or our love for him.[[fn:1]] Probably both belong together. God’s love reaches its goal when it is seen in his people, and in that sense love is the visible sign of an invisible God.

fear.body: These verses are about confidence on the day of judgement. John does not say that our love must be flawless before we can be confident; if he did, none of us could be. He says that where God’s love has really taken hold, the fear of being punished loses its grip, because sin has been dealt with (see 4:10). The fear he means is the dread of punishment, not reverent respect for God.

together.header: Key idea: faith, love and obedience belong together
together.body: In 5:1–5 John ties three things together. Believing that Jesus is the Christ shows that we are born of God. Those born of God love God and his children. Loving God means keeping his commands, and these are not a heavy burden to those born of him. Faith, love and obedience are not three separate tasks. They are signs of one new life, and the faith that trusts Jesus is also what wins the victory over the world (5:4–5).

footnotes.body: Some older English Bibles add extra words in verse 7 about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit. They are not found in the earliest Greek manuscripts, and the NET and most modern translations leave them out.

In verse 16 the NET says ‘fellow Christian’; John’s word is ‘brother’. John also does not forbid prayer for the sin that results in death: he says that he is not telling his readers to pray about it. Commentators differ about whether this is a prohibition or only a refusal to require it.

In verse 18 the NET reads ‘God protects the one he has fathered’. Many translations and commentators instead take ‘the one born of God’ to be Jesus, who keeps the believer safe, and some older translations have the believer keeping himself. Either way, the believer is kept safe by God.

witnesses.body:
John says that Jesus came by water and by blood, and not by water only, and that the Spirit, the water and the blood agree in their testimony. What do the water and the blood stand for? The most widely held view is that they mean his baptism and his death. On that view John is answering teaching that the heavenly Christ was with Jesus at the start of his ministry but left before the cross; John insists that Jesus Christ is one person, and that his death mattered. A less common view takes the water to refer to Jesus’ ministry as the one who baptises with the Holy Spirit (John 1:33), set beside his death. Either way, John’s point is that the testimony about Jesus is solid, and that the cross is not an optional extra.[[fn:1]]

Under the law, a matter was established by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and John may have that idea in mind.

knowing.body:
Verse 13 is the nearest thing to a statement of purpose in the letter. John has written so that those who believe in the Son of God may know that they have eternal life. Not hope, not guess: know.

I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life. (1 John 5:13, NET)

What is that knowledge based on? Not on a feeling. John points to what God has said about his Son (5:9–12), to the Spirit’s witness, and to the marks he has described through the letter: believing that Jesus is the Christ, obeying God and loving other believers. These marks do two things. They reassure those who are trusting Christ and show that their trust is real; and they warn anyone who claims to know God while living against what the letter says. So they also invite honest self-examination, but always so that we look to Christ and are assured by him. They are not meant to produce anxiety, or to let us build a case for ourselves.

prayer.header: Praying in line with his will (5:14–15)
prayer.body: ‘According to his will’ is not a loophole for answered prayer, and it is not a test of how much faith we have. It describes the confidence of children who know their Father and want what he wants. Praying this way does not bend God to our plans; it brings us into line with his. John follows at once with a concrete case: praying for a fellow believer who sins (5:16).

sinDeath.body:
John says that if we see a fellow believer sinning, we should pray, and God will give that person life, provided the sin is not one resulting in death. About that sin he says only that he is not telling us to pray about it. He does not say what it is, so Christians have understood it in different ways.

ReadingWhat it holdsDifficulty
Physical deathGod may discipline a believer’s serious sin with death (compare Acts 5:1–11 and 1 Corinthians 11:30)John sets it against ‘life’, which points to spiritual rather than bodily life
A particular unforgivable sinA specific sin, such as blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, or a list of ‘deadly’ sinsJohn names none, and nothing in the letter suggests a list
A true believer falling awayA real Christian can commit a sin that cuts them off from lifeJohn says that the one born of God does not go on sinning and is kept safe (5:18), and that believers have life (5:12–13)
Final rejection of ChristThe settled denial of the Son by people who have left and were never truly his (2:19)Fits the letter best, but John does not say how anyone is to recognise it

This study takes the last reading as the most probable. It fits John’s concerns throughout the letter, and it does not suggest that a true Christian can lose the life God has given. But Christians have held every one of these views, and nothing here asks you to settle the matter.[[fn:2]]

One thing is not in doubt: John is writing to reassure. His concern is with those who have turned from Christ, not with Christians who are troubled about their sin. If you are truly distressed about this, speak with a pastor or a mature Christian friend.

closing.body:
The letter closes with three statements that begin ‘we know’: that those born of God do not go on sinning, that we belong to God while the whole world lies in the power of the evil one, and that the Son of God has come and given us understanding so that we know the true God. John holds the believer and the world apart here as he has done all through the letter, and the first certainty repeats the point of 3:9.[[fn:3]]

Then comes an abrupt warning to keep away from idols (5:21). After describing Jesus as the true God and eternal life, John’s last word is that nothing, whether a false christ, a comfortable religion or anything else, can be allowed to stand beside him.
